What makes selling a house in Elizabeth, NJ different from other Union County towns?

Elizabeth is a dense port city: 141,675 residents on 12.32 square miles of land, about 11,145 people per square mile by the 2020 count. Only 25.6 percent of homes are owner occupied, so many houses for sale are two, three and four family buildings that investors and live-in owners both compete for. Median value of owner-occupied homes is $449,300 for 2020 to 2024, and median household income is $66,555.

That mix shapes what buyers ask about. Median gross rent is $1,523, and the household count is 46,121 at 2.95 people each.

Where is Elizabeth, and how is it laid out?

The city sits in Union County between Newark to the north and Linden to the southwest, with Roselle, Roselle Park, Union and Hillside to the west. Newark Bay and the Arthur Kill form its eastern edge, and the Goethals Bridge lands here on the way to Staten Island. The Elizabeth River runs 4.2 miles through the city, mostly in a channel.

The street plan is unusual for New Jersey. Instead of a grid, it is largely circular, with streets radiating from the central railroad station. A buyer driving the neighborhoods will notice that a house a block from Elizabeth station and one near Warinanco Park are very different propositions.

Which Elizabeth neighborhoods do buyers talk about?

Elizabeth neighborhoods and their housing character
NeighborhoodWhat it is known for
Midtown / UptownMain commercial district with churches from the Revolutionary era, the 1931 Art Deco Hersch Tower and the Ritz Theatre
BaywaySouthern end beside Linden; older, well kept homes, many affordable two to four family buildings, a long-standing Polish community

Because housing type changes block by block, a good listing names the neighborhood and the number of units in the first line.

What does the city require before an Elizabeth house can be sold?

Elizabeth has an online Resale Certificates application, and the form asks you to attach the smoke detector certificate if the property is occupied. Ask the City of Elizabeth for the current fee and inspection timing when you submit it.

The city's published detector rules give you a checklist to work from before you apply:

  • Smoke detectors on every level, including the basement and any finished attic, mounted at the center of the ceiling within ten feet of bedrooms.
  • A carbon monoxide detector on every floor near sleeping areas, with combination units allowed.
  • A UL listed 2-A:10-B:C fire extinguisher, fully charged and mounted within ten feet of the stove in every kitchen.
  • Hardwired systems must have power on and all units sounding together; battery units cannot replace a hardwired system.

Everything has to be mounted and working before the inspector arrives.

How do schools, transit and roads affect Elizabeth sales?

Elizabeth Public Schools is one of 31 former Abbott districts, and the state covers school construction costs there. It ran 36 schools and 28,712 students in 2018-19, Five new academies and a smaller Elizabeth High School came out of a split that began in 2009-10, when the old school had 5,300 students.

Transit is a real draw. NJ Transit stops at Elizabeth station and North Elizabeth on the Northeast Corridor and North Jersey Coast lines, with service to Newark Penn, Secaucus Junction and New York Penn. Buses run to the Port Authority terminal and to Newark. By road, the New Jersey Turnpike, Interstate 278, U.S. 1 and 9, and Routes 27, 28, 81 and 439 all cross the city. The Port Newark Elizabeth Marine Terminal and part of Newark Liberty airport sit within the city, and The Mills at Jersey Gardens anchors retail.

The Census says mean travel to work is 26.7 minutes.

What do the Census figures say about Elizabeth buyers and sellers?

The population estimate rose 3.2 percent between April 2020 and July 2025, from a base of 137,306 to 141,675. Foreign-born residents make up 51.6 percent of the city, 77.1 percent of people over five speak a language other than English at home, and 67.4 percent identify as Hispanic or Latino. Persons per household average 2.95.

  • A bilingual listing, flyer and contract summary reaches more of those buyers.
  • Only 14.6 percent of adults 25 and older hold a bachelor's degree, while 74.2 percent have finished high school.
  • Retail sales were about $14,019 per resident in 2022.

Use these numbers to price realistically against the $449,300 median rather than against figures from richer Union County suburbs.

What is Elizabeth's history, and does it touch a sale?

English settlers founded Elizabethtown in 1664, and it served as New Jersey's first capital. The state legislature created the City of Elizabeth in 1855 and Union County was formed in 1857. The Singer Sewing Machine plant in Elizabethport once employed thousands, and the company left in 1982.

Elizabethport, the oldest neighborhood, grew around businesses serving ships, and Bayway grew up around the refinery on the Linden line. Whatever the age of your building, gather permit records and any boiler, roof or electrical paperwork before you list.

What should an Elizabeth seller gather before listing?

  • The current block and lot numbers, confirmed with the Tax Assessor, since the city renumbered parcels starting January 1, 2023.
  • Proof of working, mounted detectors and extinguishers for every unit, ready for the smoke certificate attached to the resale application.
  • Permit records for any finished basement, converted attic or added unit.
  • Tenant names, lease terms and security deposit records if the building is occupied.
  • The deed, mortgage payoff figure and any lien letters.

Having all of this in one folder shortens the time between accepting an offer and sending a contract package to the buyer's attorney.

How are deeds and closing handled for an Elizabeth property?

Deeds are recorded with the Union County Clerk, whose land records site is clerk.ucnj.org. A notice there says the city began assigning new lot and block numbers on January 1, 2023, and that the person preparing the deed must confirm the correct numbers with the Tax Assessor or the county tax board association before recording. The clerk is not responsible for numbers copied from an old document.

On the state side, the seller pays the realty transfer fee on the deed. Rates run per $500 of price and step up in bands, and sales over $1,000,000 add a graduated percent fee. A seller who is a New Jersey resident signs GIT/REP-3. Sellers who are nonresidents use GIT/REP-1 or GIT/REP-2 unless a listed assurance applies. Appeals of an assessment must reach the county board of taxation by April 1.

More questions about Elizabeth, NJ

Do I need an inspection to sell my Elizabeth house?

Yes, Elizabeth runs a resale certificate program through an online application, and an occupied house needs its smoke detector certificate attached. Ask the city's Bureau of Zoning for the current fee and the inspection schedule.

What does Elizabeth require for detectors and extinguishers?

Smoke detectors on every level, carbon monoxide detectors on every floor near bedrooms, and a charged 2-A:10-B:C extinguisher within ten feet of the stove in each kitchen. All must be permanently mounted and working.

Which county office records an Elizabeth deed?

The Union County Clerk. Check the block and lot numbers first, because the city issued new ones starting January 1, 2023.

How many people live in Elizabeth?

What should a seller know about Englewood, NJ before listing?

The inspection is short, but the permit check that comes first can take longer than the visit itself, so begin early.

Census figures for 2020 to 2024 show a median owner-occupied home value of $544,100, median household income of $102,571, and 54.5 percent of homes owner occupied. The city has 11,274 households and 5,951 people per square mile,.

How does the Englewood Certificate of Continued Occupancy work?

City Ordinance 85-40, in Chapter 9 of the Revised General Ordinances, says a seller must receive a CCO before ownership transfers. New construction and buildings the state inspects, such as hotels and rooming houses, are outside it. The city's stated purpose is to check safety and to hand the new owner information about fire and occupancy rules.

  1. Once you have a buyer, the seller or agent visits the Englewood Municipal Building at 2-10 North Van Brunt Street, second floor, and tells the Building Department about the sale.
  2. Any open permits for work on the property must be closed out before an inspection can be scheduled.
  3. The application asks for the property address, owner and buyer contact details, the buyer's present address (or a mailing address for an LLC or corporation), and the number of people living there before and after the sale.
  4. You pay the fee to the City of Englewood and the inspector visits.
  5. The certificate is passed to the buyer at closing.

Selling without a CCO risks fines and delays at the closing table.

What happens if the inspector finds an illegal unit or unpermitted work?

The owner has to remove the extra unit, which means cutting off utility service and removing the added kitchen and bathroom. The certificate issues only after a second inspection confirms the work is done and the code is met. Work that needed a permit and did not get one must go through the Building Department first.

If you suspect an old basement apartment or an attic conversion has no paperwork, talk to the Building Department before you accept a contract. Raising it early leaves time to renegotiate before the closing date is fixed.

What is Englewood like, and who buys here?

Englewood borders Bergenfield, Englewood Cliffs, Fort Lee, Leonia, Teaneck and Tenafly, and Highwood is an unincorporated community inside its lines. The area was part of the English Neighborhood during the colonial era, and street names such as Brinckerhoff, Van Brunt, Lydecker, Demarest and Van Nostrand recall the Dutch, Huguenot and English families who settled it.

  • Four of the city's five National Register sites are houses on Grand Avenue: the Benson, Demarest, Lydecker and Demott-Westervelt houses. The fifth is St. Paul's Episcopal Church on Engle Street.
  • Flat Rock Brook is a 150 acre preserve on Van Nostrand Avenue with 3.6 miles of trails, and MacKay Park on North Van Brunt Street has a pool, rink and athletic fields.
  • Englewood Hospital sits on Engle Street.

Residents in the Census data are 32.2 percent White alone, 20.4 percent Black alone, 14.9 percent Asian alone, and 33.5 percent Hispanic or Latino, and 36.4 percent of people were born abroad.

  • Adults 25 and older with a bachelor's degree or higher make up 46.5 percent.

Compare your carrying costs against those medians when deciding how long to wait for an offer.

Where did Englewood begin?

The Lenape, of the turtle clan, lived here first; a population of about 2,000 had dwindled to 50 by 1832. Henry Hudson's 1607 voyage let the Netherlands claim the watershed, but settlement picked up only after England took New Netherland in 1664. The Garret Lydecker House on Grand Avenue dates to 1808.

Whatever your house's age, the CCO inspector reads any addition or conversion as a permit question.

How do commuting and schools factor into an Englewood sale?

Interstate 95 clips the city for 0.43 miles near the Leonia line. Routes 4 and 93 and county routes 501 and 505 carry local traffic. NJ Transit bus 166 runs to the Port Authority Bus Terminal, while routes 171, 175, 178 and 186 serve the George Washington Bridge Bus Station, and Rockland Coaches also runs to Port Authority. Passenger trains on the Erie Northern Branch served Englewood from 1859 until 1966, and a proposed light rail extension would add stops at Englewood Route 4, Englewood Town Center and the hospital. Mean travel time to work is 30.9 minutes.

The Englewood Public School District had 2,955 students in five schools for 2023-24, from the D. A. Quarles Early Childhood Center to Dwight Morrow High School, which also takes students from Englewood Cliffs. Bergen County students can apply to the Bergen County Academies and other county technical programs, and the city has the Englewood on the Palisades Charter School.

What are the state steps at the deed, and where does it get recorded?

Bergen County's Clerk acts as the recording officer for deeds, mortgages and liens. The state charges the seller a realty transfer fee on the deed, and any price above $350,000 uses a higher schedule: for example, $4.80 per $500 on the slice between $200,000 and $550,000. Sales above $1,000,000 add a graduated percent fee that starts at 1 percent.

A resident seller signs the state's GIT/REP-3 form for recording, and nonresident sellers use GIT/REP-1 or GIT/REP-2 unless a stated assurance applies. For a tax assessment challenge, the county board of taxation must receive your petition by April 1, or May 1 where a revaluation or reassessment took place.

Yes. City Ordinance 85-40 requires a Certificate of Continued Occupancy for one, two and multi-family houses before ownership changes hands.

$150 for a one or two family home and $250 for a multi-family building, paid to the City of Englewood with the application.

A working smoke detector on each level, a working carbon monoxide detector within 10 feet of bedrooms, and an ABC extinguisher of 2 to 10 pounds within 10 feet of the kitchen.

At the Building Department, second floor of the Municipal Building, 2-10 North Van Brunt Street. Have the buyer's name, phone and address ready, and close out any open permits first.

Fair Lawn is a Bergen County borough about 12 miles northwest of New York City, and the Census counted 34,927 people there in 2020. The Census Bureau's July 2025 estimate is 37,128, a gain of 6.3 percent over the 2020 base. The borough covers only 5.14 square miles of land, so density is around 6,800 people per square mile and houses sit close together.

What is Fair Lawn's history, and how does it show in the housing?

Fair Lawn was farmland before it was a suburb, and the oldest houses on Berdan Avenue and Fair Lawn Avenue still reflect that. Dutch and Irish settlers divided the land into large farm lots in colonial times, and Victorian homes went up along Berdan Avenue beside five Berdan family farms. The borough takes its name from Fairlawn, the estate David Acker built in 1865, which later became the Fair Lawn Municipal Building.

Residents petitioned to leave Saddle River Township because they felt the schools were poor value for the taxes they paid, and Fair Lawn became its own borough in 1924. Suburban growth came in three pockets: Memorial Park around River Road and Fair Lawn Avenue, Columbus Heights at Lincoln Avenue and Wagaraw Road, and Warren Point east of the railroad and south of Broadway.

Radburn, founded in 1929 as a town for the motor age, is one of the first planned communities in the United States and lies inside the borough. Eight sites in Fair Lawn are on the National Register of Historic Places, including the Radburn station and the Naugle House on Dunkerhook Road. If a buyer will do the repairs, the borough offers a Conditional Certificate for transfer of title only, with no occupancy. The buyer's attorney must send a letter confirming the buyer understands that, and after closing the buyer reapplies for the full certificate, paying another $175. On an as-is sale, the buyer must acknowledge that anything the inspection finds becomes the buyer's responsibility to correct.

How does the grid address system affect a Fair Lawn listing?

Most Fair Lawn addresses use a hyphenated number, such as the library's 10-01 Fair Lawn Avenue, and buyers who search online sometimes get no match unless they leave the dash out. Nearly 10,000 Fair Lawn addresses use this system, which accounts for almost half of the hyphenated addresses in New Jersey.

The first number tells you the block distance from Broadway on north-south streets, or the numbered street on east-west ones. Addresses south of Broadway or Route 4 begin with a zero. The system dates to at least the 1930s and was designed so emergency crews could find a house fast. Exceptions exist on the Glen Rock, Hawthorne and Saddle Brook sides and inside Radburn.

When you advertise the house, write the address both with and without the dash, and confirm it on the tax record so title and survey work match what appears on the deed.

Which roads, trains and neighborhoods define Fair Lawn?

Fair Lawn works as a commuter town because of two stations and two highways. Route 4 reaches the George Washington Bridge in under 10 miles from the Broadway district, and Route 208 runs northwest to Interstate 287. The Radburn and Broadway stations on NJ Transit's Bergen County Line serve Hoboken, with connections at Secaucus Junction to New York Penn Station. NJ Transit buses 144, 145, 148, 160, 164 and 196 run to the Port Authority Bus Terminal.

Local roads form a rough three-by-three grid: Saddle River Road, Plaza Road and River Road run north to south, and Broadway, Morlot Avenue and Fair Lawn Avenue run east to west. The borough had about 99.6 miles of roadway in 2010, 84 of them municipal.

  • Berdan Grove: single-family streets around Berdan Grove Park, with the borough's highest concentration of Asian American residents.
  • Broadway District: the main shopping strip and a train stop at Warren Point and Lyncrest.
  • Radburn: the planned community with its own station and pathways.
  • Parks: Memorial Park, Berdan Grove Park, Gregory Park and Cresthill Park.

Which schools serve Fair Lawn, and who employs its residents?

Fair Lawn Public Schools run from prekindergarten through twelfth grade, with nine schools and 5,529 students in 2022 to 2023. Elementary schools are Forrest, Lyncrest, Milnes, Radburn, Warren Point and Westmoreland for kindergarten through fourth grade, and Memorial and Thomas Jefferson middle schools cover grades 5 to 8. Fair Lawn High School had 1,624 students and has been recognized as a Blue Ribbon School.

Employers include Columbia Bank, headquartered in the borough, Kuiken Brothers building materials, Zerega's pasta, and U.S. Technologies. The large Nabisco and Mondelez bakery on Route 208 operated from 1958 and was announced for closure in 2021, with demolition beginning in January 2023. The Fair Lawn Promenade, a mixed-use complex, opened on April 1, 2014. The Broadway shopping district continues to supply local retail jobs.

What are the closing steps and costs in Fair Lawn?

The seller pays the state Realty Transfer Fee when the Bergen County Clerk records the deed, and for a sale over $350,000 the fee runs from $2.90 per $500 on the first $150,000 up to $4.80 on the band from $200,000 to $550,000 and $5.30 per $500 between $550,000 and $850,000. Over $1 million, a graduated percent fee also falls on the seller, and your attorney will calculate it.

Sellers who are New Jersey residents, including estates and trusts, complete a GIT/REP-3 to record the deed. For an estate sale, the executors who sign the deed also sign the form, and an executor who is also a beneficiary signs two forms. County clerks decide whether to accept a deed, so a rejection should be resolved with the clerk's office first, then with the state GIT/REP Unit at 609-322-9275.

Property tax appeals in Bergen County go to the Board of Taxation at 201-336-6300, and its page says the filing deadline for 2026 assessment appeals has passed. For rent control questions on a rented house, the borough's rent leveling office is at (201) 564-6152.

Can a buyer take a Fair Lawn house that fails the inspection?

Yes, with a Conditional Certificate for transfer of title only. The buyer's attorney must send a letter confirming that the buyer understands there is no occupancy, and a failed sidewalk must still be fixed. After closing, the buyer reapplies for the full certificate and pays another $175.

Who signs the GIT/REP form when an estate sells a Fair Lawn house?

The estate completes the form, signed by the executors who sign the deed or by the administrator if there is no will. An executor who is also a beneficiary signs two forms, one for the estate and one personally. Residents use the GIT/REP-3.

Why do Fair Lawn addresses have a dash?

The dash comes from the borough's grid numbering system, in use since at least the 1930s. The first number counts blocks from Broadway or follows the numbered street, and addresses south of Broadway start with a zero. Many online forms only accept the number without the dash.

Which county office records a Fair Lawn deed?

The Bergen County Clerk records deeds, and the Bergen County Board of Taxation handles assessment appeals. The state Realty Transfer Fee and the GIT/REP form go in with the deed. Ask your closing attorney or title company to confirm the filing method for your closing date.

How did Fort Lee get here, and does the history matter to a sale?

Fort Lee began as a Revolutionary War outpost, then became the first center of American filmmaking, and later a skyline of residential towers. Fort Constitution was renamed Fort Lee after General Charles Lee, and in November 1776 Thomas Paine wrote The American Crisis while retreating along what is now Main Street. The New Jersey Legislature formed the borough on March 29, 1904 from remaining parts of Ridgefield Township.

Kalem began filming in Fort Lee in 1907, the Champion Film Company built the first studio in 1909, and many more studios followed during the 1910s and 1920s. The Barrymore Film Center, a theater and film museum that cost $16 million, opened in October 2022.

High-rise apartment construction along Palisade Avenue and Boulevard East began in the 1960s and raised the borough's density sharply. As of 2019 ten structures here, including the bridge, stood over 300 feet. Two 47-story towers called The Modern, finished in 2014 and 2018, are among Bergen County's tallest buildings. What local paperwork does Fort Lee ask of sellers?

How do condos, co-ops and associations affect a Fort Lee sale?

How do Fort Lee's roads and transit affect buyers?

Fort Lee's position at the George Washington Bridge shapes how buyers judge a property. The bridge, signed as I-95, U.S. 1-9 and U.S. 46, is the world's busiest motor vehicle bridge and carries traffic to Washington Heights in Upper Manhattan.

Roads through the borough include Route 4, Route 5, Route 67, U.S. 9W, U.S. 1/9, U.S. 46, County Route 505, the Palisades Interstate Parkway and Interstate 95. The borough had about 51 miles of roadway in 2010, and the municipality maintained roughly 35 of them.

Cole Middle School for grades 5 to 8, and Fort Lee High School. School 3 won a National Blue Ribbon award in 2010 to 2011. Students can also apply to Bergen County Technical Schools, including the Bergen County Academies in Hackensack.

The borough's named communities include Coytesville, Linwood, Palisade and Taylorville, along with the Palisade Avenue and Boulevard East tower corridor and downtown Main Street. Fort Lee Koreatown, a dining district since the mid-1980s, is a draw for visitors, and Monument Park hosts summer outdoor Shakespeare shows.

Cliffside Park, Edgewater, Englewood, Englewood Cliffs, Leonia, Palisades Park and Ridgefield border the borough. A buyer comparing prices will look at those towns too, so keep your asking price consistent with nearby recent sales.

What are the closing costs and filings for a Fort Lee sale?

Just 44.7% of households own their home (2020-2024), compared with 69.3% in Franklin Township, Somerset County. Median home value sits at $475,500 and median gross rent at $1,688. With that split, a Garfield seller tends to see two buyer types: an occupant, and an investor who plans to rent the units out.

Both buyer types face the same city paperwork before title passes. The sections below take it in order, beginning with the resale certificate Garfield asks for on every sale.

How did Garfield take shape as a city?

Garfield began as a handful of houses and became a city within 44 years. Gilbert D. Bogart put up the first seven homes in 1873 in what was then called East Passaic. The community took the name Garfield in 1881, became a borough in 1898 and turned into a city on April 19, 1917, after a referendum.

The city shares land borders with Elmwood Park, Lodi, Saddle Brook and South Hackensack, and the Saddle River separates it from Wallington. Old neighborhood names such as Belmont, Bogart Heights, Dundee Dam and Plauderville still appear on deeds and listings.

One piece of local history matters for diligence. The EPA identified groundwater contamination from a 1983 chromic acid spill at a former electroplating company in Garfield and announced a $37 million cleanup in 2016. Buyers and lenders sometimes ask about nearby cleanup sites, so look up your street in the EPA's records early.

What does Garfield require before a house can be resold?

Garfield requires a certificate of occupancy for resale plus a separate smoke, carbon monoxide and fire extinguisher certification. The city's own instruction sheet says to submit the request through the Building Department citizen portal or by email, then wait for the email that tells you when fees are due.

The sheet also gives a timeline and a warning. Processing is listed as 10 business days from the day the application is received, and sellers are told not to schedule a closing until the certificate is in hand. Ignoring the ordinance can bring a fine of $2,000.

  • Send the property address and the full names, current home addresses, phone numbers and emails of buyer and seller. Do not list a business, attorney or real estate office address.
  • If an LLC or corporation is selling, give the contact person's details as well.
  • For an estate sale, attach the Surrogate letter to the application.
  • Pay the certificate fee to the City of Garfield and the smoke certification fee to the Bureau of Fire Prevention, each with its own check or money order.

The fees are charged by building type, and the city asks sellers to wait for its fee email before paying.

Garfield resale fees listed on the city's instruction sheet
Building typeCertificate of occupancySmoke and CO certification
One-family$50$50
Two-family$100$100
Three or more units$100 for the first two units, $25 per added unit$100 for the first two units, $25 per added unit

How do tenants, repairs or an open estate change a Garfield sale?

Each of these situations adds one step to the process without blocking it. An as-is house can still receive its paperwork once the smoke and fire items pass.

The detector rules are specific. Under the city's dwelling certificate sheet, ten-year sealed-battery smoke alarms and carbon monoxide alarms must sit within ten feet of every bedroom, and a common stairwell needs smoke alarms at the top and bottom. Inspectors also ask for access to the attic and basement.

  • A tenant-occupied house may also need a dwelling certificate. Ordinance 2213 requires one on any change of occupancy, with a $60 fee per unit that includes the smoke certification, unless an inspection happened within the previous eleven months.
  • A second visit costs another $60 per unit if the unit fails or the paperwork is not on site.
  • For a house with a deceased owner, the application asks for the Surrogate letter, so have it ready before you apply.

If repairs are the problem, fix the detector items first. They are the cheapest part of the checklist, and the city's sheet cites the state rule at N.J.A.C. 5:70-2.3 for them.

What state paperwork gets recorded with a Garfield deed?

The Bergen County Clerk records a Garfield deed, and the state attaches two filings to it: the Realty Transfer Fee and a gross income tax residency form. Under the Division of Taxation's description, the seller owes the fee and it is computed from the consideration recited in the deed.

For prices of $350,000 or less, the schedule starts at $2.00 per $500 of the first $150,000 and tops out at $3.90 per $500 for the slice between $200,000 and $350,000. A higher schedule applies above $350,000, opening at $2.90 per $500 and reaching $4.80 per $500 for the slice from $200,000 to $550,000.

The state lists exemptions for deeds between husband and wife or parent and child, and for an executor's deed distributing an estate to an heir. An arm's-length purchase does not fit any of them.

The residency paperwork is the GIT/REP. A New Jersey resident signs the GIT/REP-3. A nonresident seller prepays estimated gross income tax, never less than 2% of the deed consideration, unless a listed assurance on the form applies. According to the Division's FAQ, no deed gets recorded without a signed GIT/REP-1, -2 or -3.

What do Garfield schools, roads and transit offer a buyer?

Garfield sells on access: two NJ Transit rail stops and Route 46 both sit inside the city. The Garfield and Plauderville stations on the Bergen County Line run to Hoboken Terminal, with a transfer at Secaucus Junction for Penn Station. NJ Transit buses 160 and 161 run to Midtown Manhattan's Port Authority terminal.

By road, U.S. Route 46 and County Route 507 pass through, and Midland Avenue, Outwater Lane, River Drive and Passaic Street are the other main streets. Mean commute time for workers is 28.0 minutes (2020-2024).

The public schools are the Garfield Public Schools, a pre-K to grade 12 district with 12 schools and 4,713 students in 2020-21, one of the state's former Abbott districts. Garfield High School enrolled 1,159 students that year. Residents can also apply to the Bergen County Technical Schools, including the Bergen County Academies in Hackensack. A buyer with children will ask about these, so have the district name ready.

Which sale route fits a Garfield owner best?

Your deadline and the condition of the building decide it. Listing reaches the most buyers but puts showings and repair requests on you. A private sale or cash buyer trims the repair list, yet the city certificate and fire certification apply to all three.

  • List with an agent if the building is in good order and you can wait on a buyer's mortgage approval.
  • Sell privately if a buyer is already lined up, such as a tenant, relative or neighbor.
  • Consider a cash offer for a building that needs work, carries tenants or belongs to an estate, and settle in the contract who orders the certificate and pays the $50 or $100 city fee.

Fix the closing date first, then count back 10 business days to learn the last day to file with the city.

More questions about Garfield, NJ

Is an inspection mandatory when I sell in Garfield?

Yes. Garfield requires a certificate of occupancy for resale and a smoke, carbon monoxide and fire extinguisher certification. The city lists 10 business days for processing and tells sellers not to schedule a closing before the certificate is issued.

How much is the Garfield resale certificate?

One-family houses pay $50 and two-family houses pay $100 on the city's sheet. Bigger buildings pay $100 for two units plus $25 for each one after that. The Bureau of Fire Prevention charges its smoke and CO certification on the same scale.

Who pays the New Jersey realty transfer fee in a Garfield sale?

The seller pays it. The county recording officer collects the state fee at recording, and the amount scales with the price in the deed. Spouse-to-spouse and parent-to-child deeds carry an exemption.

Can I sell a Garfield house that I inherited and have not cleared up yet?

Yes, once you have the right papers. Garfield wants the Surrogate letter with the certificate application on an estate sale. Selling to an outside buyer is a taxable transfer, though an executor's deed to an heir is exempt.

Do I need a dwelling certificate if tenants live in the house?

Possibly. City Ordinance 2213 calls for a dwelling certificate on a change of occupancy, at $60 per unit, unless the unit was inspected in the previous eleven months. Ask the Fire Prevention Bureau whether your tenant situation triggers it.

What is the quickest way to move a house in Hackensack?

The quickest sale is the one with the fewest open items at the start: a passed fire inspection, a clear tax balance and a price grounded in recent Hackensack sales. Hackensack is the Bergen County seat and the county's largest municipality, home to 46,030 people in 2020 and an estimated 46,380 by July 1, 2025.

Only 36.6 percent of homes are lived in by their owners, which tells you that renting dominates the housing stock. An owner of a two-family house or a small building should plan on tenants, leases and rent questions arising during the sale. Agents, private sales and cash buyers all follow the same city inspection, tax payoff and recording steps. A cash buyer simply removes the lender's appraisal and approval from the timeline.

What kind of housing does Hackensack offer?

The city sits about 12 miles northwest of Midtown Manhattan on 4.35 square miles, and each block can differ from the next. Wikipedia's description lists a residential high-rise strip about a mile long on Prospect Avenue, single-family streets covering roughly a third of the city (mostly west), older two-family neighborhoods, big garden apartment complexes and a small-city downtown.

Hackensack University Medical Center, the Bergen County Court House, Fairleigh Dickinson University's Metropolitan Campus and a Bergen Community College site fill out the map. Bordering towns are Bogota, Hasbrouck Heights, Little Ferry, Lodi, Maywood, Paramus, Ridgefield Park, River Edge, South Hackensack, Teaneck and Teterboro.

  • West side: single-family homes, some on lots of an acre or more.
  • Older central blocks: two-family houses.
  • Prospect Avenue and the garden complexes: apartment living at scale.
  • Downtown and small neighborhood business districts: mixed-use buildings.

Which Hackensack figures should shape my asking price?

Hackensack pairs a renter-heavy population with a large tax bill: the average home was billed $10,307 in 2025. The table lines up the numbers that matter when you set a price.

Hackensack at a glance, from Census Bureau and state tax division data

The state table for 2025 shows a general rate of 3.209 per $100 here and an effective rate of 2.527. Average sale prices in the state study ran about $75,000 above the average assessment, so base your number on nearby closed sales and not on the tax card.

Which inspection does Hackensack require before a house sale?

The Fire Prevention Bureau issues a Certificate of Smoke Alarm, Carbon Monoxide Alarm and Portable Fire Extinguisher Compliance, and a seller needs it before closing. The city's form lists a $70 fee, a six-month validity period and issuance on the day of the inspection.

If the house fails or nobody is home for the appointment, the city charges a new fee on a new application. The form wants the buyer's name, the seller's name and the real estate company, and the city warns that wrong details void the report.

The requirement traces to the state Uniform Fire Code, which calls for a smoke alarm certificate whenever a one-family or two-family dwelling is sold, leased or changes occupants. Only the municipality can issue it. Prepare the house first:

  • Smoke alarms on every level including the basement, in shared stairwells and hallways, and within 10 feet of each sleeping area.
  • Sealed ten-year battery alarms in place of old ones, since the Division of Fire Safety advises swapping alarms every decade.
  • A carbon monoxide alarm and a portable fire extinguisher, both listed on the city form.

Also ask the Building, Housing and Land Use department whether other resale paperwork applies to your type of property.

What does the Hackensack tax collector expect from a seller?

Taxes fall due on the first day of February, May, August and November, and each date carries a 10-day grace period. Late balances up to $1,500 accrue 8 percent annually, and anything above that accrues 18 percent. The collector says everything must be paid by November 10 to avoid the accelerated tax sale starting November 11.

The city's page gives a 2026 final rate of $3.530 per $100 and reports that final bills went out on September 16, 2026. New owners are warned that the county can take three to six months to record a deed and tell the city, so a buyer should send the collector a mailing address after closing. Request a written balance from the collector before you review the closing statement.

Owners who think the assessment overshoots market value can appeal to the Bergen County Board of Taxation at Two Bergen County Plaza in Hackensack. The annual filing date is April 1, and the 2026 window is over. Property assessed above $750,000 may go straight to the Tax Court by April 1.

What will a Hackensack seller pay at the closing table?

The state charges the seller a Realty Transfer Fee when the deed is recorded. Using the state's rate table for sales above $350,000, a $400,000 sale produces a fee near $3,215. A graduated percent fee applies above $1,000,000, and the state's page lists that schedule.

  • The state transfer fee, collected at recording.
  • The $70 fire certificate.
  • Mortgage payoff and any recorded liens.
  • The seller's portion of the quarter's property tax.

Resident sellers sign the GIT/REP-3 residency certification so the clerk will take the deed. Out-of-state sellers prepay Gross Income Tax, with a floor of 2 percent of the sale price unless a listed assurance covers them. An executor's deed to an heir named in the will falls under the state's list of exempt transfers.

How should a landlord handle a Hackensack rental sale?

Roughly 63 percent of occupied homes here are rented, and typical rent is $1,911. The Department of Building, Housing and Land Use also staffs the Rent Stabilization Board, so check with that office on whether your building is covered before you price from market rents.

The state fire certificate applies to leases as well as sales, so a tenant turnover and a sale may each need an inspection. Book the inspection late enough that the six-month certificate still covers your closing date.

How do Hackensack's roads and rail lines influence demand?

Interstate 80, Route 17, Route 4 and County Route 503 cross the city, and bridges at Court Street, Midtown and Anderson Street span the Hackensack River. The city counted 79.69 miles of roadway in 2010, with 62.10 city-maintained, 15.10 county-maintained and 2.49 state-maintained.

The Pascack Valley Line stops at Anderson Street and Essex Street on its way to Hoboken and connections to Penn Station New York. Buses leave the Hackensack Bus Terminal for the Port Authority and the George Washington Bridge Bus Station. A listing close to a station or the terminal puts that commute in front of buyers.

More questions about Hackensack, NJ

Is a fire inspection certificate mandatory for a Hackensack sale?

Yes. State rules require a smoke alarm certificate for one-family and two-family sales, and the city fire bureau issues it for $70 on a form that also covers carbon monoxide alarms and a portable fire extinguisher. It stays valid for six months.

What would the state transfer fee be on a $400,000 Hackensack sale?

About $3,215 by the state's schedule for prices above $350,000. The seller pays it at recording, and exemptions are limited to the transfers the state lists, such as a deed between parent and child.

Does a Hackensack house with unpaid taxes still sell?

It can, once the balance is cleared at or before closing. The city wants current-year taxes paid by November 10 to avoid the tax sale that begins November 11, and late balances accrue interest at 8 percent up to $1,500 and 18 percent above.

May I sell while tenants live in the house?

Yes, a tenant-occupied house can sell. Ask the Building, Housing and Land Use department about rent stabilization and have an attorney read every lease, because the buyer steps into the occupancy.

What changes when the house came through an estate?

The estate signs a GIT/REP form for its residency status, and an executor's deed to an heir named in the will is exempt from the transfer fee. A sale to an outside buyer is taxed, and the fire certificate is still required.

What are the quickest ways to sell a house in Hoboken, New Jersey?

Hoboken sellers can list on the open market, sell on their own or take a cash offer from a buyer who purchases as-is. The right one depends on what you own: a condo unit, a rowhouse or a small building with tenants each hit different city offices.

The city's housing stock is dense and mostly renter-occupied, so many sales involve a lease, a registration or a rent ordinance. Sorting those out first shortens the path to a closing date more than any price cut would.

  • Traditional listing: strongest for a renovated unit in good condition, with showings, inspections and a buyer's financing to schedule.
  • Private sale: saves the commission, but you handle disclosures, contracts and the city's resale certificate yourself.
  • Cash purchase: suits a unit with deferred repairs, tenants in place or a deadline, since there is no mortgage approval to wait for.

What is Hoboken's layout and how did the city develop?

Hoboken sits on the west bank of the Hudson River in Hudson County, directly across from Manhattan's West Village and Chelsea. It is called the Mile Square City, though it holds about 1.25 square miles of land and 0.75 square miles of water, for a total of 2 square miles. The ZIP code is 07030.

The street plan is a grid. North-south streets carry names such as Washington, Adams, Jefferson, Madison, Monroe and Jackson, while the numbered east-west streets begin near Observer Highway and end around 16th Street by Weehawken Cove. The Northwest section, once industrial, has been rezoned and rebuilt as housing.

Dutch colonists settled the area in the 17th century, and Hoboken became a township in 1849 and a city in 1855. A steam ferry began running to Manhattan in 1811, and later the rail terminal and shipping lines tied the city to the Port of New York and New Jersey. Maxwell House, Lipton and Hostess once operated here, and the old factory blocks are now condominiums and shops.

What do Census numbers say about Hoboken housing?

Hoboken's 2020 to 2024 estimates show a city of renters with high incomes and high home values. Only about one in three housing units is owner-occupied, so a seller is often competing with a landlord market as well as other owners.

Hoboken housing and income figures, 2020 to 2024 estimates from Census QuickFacts
MeasureHoboken
Owner-occupied housing rate33.8%

The July 2025 population estimate is 59,027, down 1.7 percent from the 2020 estimates base. The 2020 count of 60,419 works out to about 48,335 people per square mile of land, and in 2010 data Hoboken ranked third in the nation for density among cities above 50,000 people.

How did Hurricane Sandy change flood questions for Hoboken sellers?

Buyers will ask about flooding, and the history gives them reason. In October 2012 Hurricane Sandy flooded about 1,700 Hoboken homes and caused roughly $100 million in damage, according to the city's encyclopedia entry, and it shut down the PATH station at Hoboken Terminal.

The response was large. The federal housing department set aside $230 million through the Rebuild by Design competition for Hoboken, Weehawken and Jersey City. The city describes a four-part plan: resist surge with barriers, delay runoff with green infrastructure, store rainwater in basins and parks, and discharge it through upgraded sewers and pump stations. Sewer separation work finished in 2022, and the second construction phase began in 2023.

The city's home page also advertises ResilienCity Park, which it calls New Jersey's largest resiliency park, able to hold up to 2 million gallons of rain. When a September 2023 storm dropped 3.5 inches of rain, the entry reports standing water of only a few inches at three of 277 intersections by evening.

If your building took water in 2012, keep repair records, flood insurance history and any elevation paperwork ready. Buyers' attorneys ask for them.

What drives Hoboken's economy and commuting?

Hoboken has the highest share of public transit commuters of any American city, with 56 percent of working residents riding each day. Hoboken Terminal in the southeast corner is a national historic landmark, built in 1907.

  • Rail and subway: NJ Transit's Main, Bergen County, Pascack Valley, Montclair-Boonton, Morris and Essex and Meadowlands lines end at the terminal, and PATH runs to 33rd Street, the World Trade Center and Journal Square.
  • Light rail, bus and ferry: the Hudson-Bergen line has three Hoboken stops, nine NJ Transit bus routes terminate at Hudson Place, and NY Waterway ferries cross to Battery Park City, Pier 11 and West Midtown.
  • Roads: the 14th Street Viaduct leads up to Jersey City Heights, and the Lincoln and Holland tunnels are nearby. The city has no airport.

Major employers include one of the John Wiley and Sons headquarters and, since 2025, a North American headquarters for Unilever at Waterfront Corporate Center. Stevens Institute of Technology supports about 1,285 full-time jobs.

Hoboken Public Schools run five schools with 3,531 students in 2023-24, and three charter schools operate separately.

Which Hoboken city rules apply when you sell or rent out a property?

Three city offices matter most: Construction Code, the Fire Department and Rent Leveling and Stabilization. City Hall is at 94 Washington Street.

Construction Code issues certificates of occupancy for new buildings, additions and altered space, and a certificate of approval for other work. The city's site also carries an application titled Certificate of Smoke Detector, CO and Fire Extinguisher Compliance, which is the form to ask about for a resale. Ask the fire inspection office whether your unit needs it.

Rent Leveling and Stabilization administers Chapter 155, the municipal rent control ordinance. Its staff answer which apartments are covered, what the legal base rent is, and how annual adjustments, vacancy decontrol and surcharges apply. Owners of single-family homes, condominiums, multiple dwellings and mixed-use buildings must register each year through the SDL portal. If you are selling a building with tenants, ask the office for the file on your property and give the buyer's attorney a copy.

How are Hoboken property taxes billed, and what do buyers and sellers owe?

Hoboken sends one tax bill with four quarterly stubs. It combines municipal, school, county and library taxes, plus a Special Improvement District assessment for properties inside that district. The office does not accept postmarks, so a payment counts only when the tax office receives it or it is paid online by the end of the grace period.

Added and omitted assessment bills for improvements go out in October and fall due November 1, with a grace period to November 10. For a lien payoff, call the Tax Collector for a redemption statement, because balances shown on the website may be wrong, and expect to pay by certified check or money order.

Appeals go to the Hudson County Board of Taxation, normally by April 1. A successful judgment is credited first to fourth-quarter taxes, then to any third-quarter balance, and any leftover is refunded to the petitioner or their attorney.

State fees matter at Hoboken prices. With a median owned-home value of $895,100, many sales approach the $1,000,000 line, above which the seller owes a graduated fee of 1 percent of the total price up to $2,000,000 and the buyer owes an extra 1 percent. Residents who keep their New Jersey residency sign GIT/REP-3 at closing instead of making an estimated payment.

More questions about Hoboken, NJ

Is there a rent control law I should know about before selling a Hoboken rental?

Yes. Hoboken enforces Chapter 155, a municipal rent control ordinance, through its Rent Leveling and Stabilization office. The office can tell you which apartments are covered, the legal base rent and the allowed increases. Owners register their properties every year through the SDL portal, and the office keeps a public file on each residential property.

Does Hoboken require a certificate to sell a home?

The city publishes an application for a Certificate of Smoke Detector, CO and Fire Extinguisher Compliance, and Construction Code issues certificates of occupancy for new or altered space. Ask the fire inspection office and your closing attorney which one your sale needs, since it can differ for a condo, a rowhouse and a multi-unit building.

Does Hoboken flood, and what should a seller have ready?

Parts of the city flooded badly in Hurricane Sandy in 2012, and the city has since built sewer, park and barrier projects with $230 million in federal funds. Buyers and their attorneys ask about past water damage, so gather repair records and insurance history for your address and review them with your attorney before listing.

When are Hoboken property taxes due?

In four quarterly installments listed on the single annual bill. The Tax Collector charges interest back to the due date once the grace period ends, and does not honor postmarks. Pay online or deliver the check to City Hall at 94 Washington Street, and call the office for a redemption figure if a lien exists.

How long do I have to appeal my Hoboken assessment?

Generally until April 1, filed with the Hudson County Board of Taxation on Form A-1. Owners of properties assessed above $1,000,000 may go straight to the Tax Court by the same date. If you disagree with the board's judgment, the Tax Court appeal must be filed within 45 days.

What should I know about selling a house in Egg Harbor Township, NJ?

Egg Harbor Township is a large Atlantic County municipality, 75.47 square miles of which 67.05 is land, and it is separate from Egg Harbor City, which has its own entry in the state's municipality lists. The Census Bureau estimates 48,435 residents for 2025. Owner-occupancy is high at 84.4 percent, the median owner-occupied home value is $312,700, and median household income is $97,190.

Both the home value and the owner share lead to one practical point for sellers: most houses here are owned, not rented, and the main pre-closing task is the state fire-safety certificate.

Does Egg Harbor Township require a smoke and carbon monoxide certificate?

New Jersey's Division of Fire Safety runs an online smoke certification application with "Change of Ownership" as a stated reason, and it asks for the closing date, block, lot and whether you are the seller or the buyer's representative. Sheriff's sales, foreclosures, forfeitures and purchases from a federal agency work differently: the new owner must obtain the certificate before moving in. A building that is uninhabitable and will be rehabilitated or demolished can be exempt from the certificate, but it cannot be occupied until a new certificate of occupancy comes from the local construction official.

For the township's own form, fee and timing, ask the Bureau of Fire Inspections before you set a closing date.

How settled is the Egg Harbor Township housing market?

Census data show a population up 1.2 percent from the April 2020 base of 47,849 to 48,435 in 2025. The township has 17,261 households averaging 2.78 people, and 93.6 percent of residents lived in the same house a year earlier.

  • Median owner costs are $2,371 a month with a mortgage and $954 without one.
  • Median gross rent is $1,456.
  • 17.7 percent of residents were born abroad, and 29.8 percent speak another language at home.
  • Veterans number 2,166.

The township's density is 713.6 people per square mile, a fraction of the Elizabeth or Englewood figure.

How did the township get its shape?

Lenape families summered near Bargaintown Lake and along Patcong Creek. A 1694 act placed the Egg Harbour settlers under Gloucester County, and Atlantic County was separated in 1837. Since then, ten municipalities have split from the original township, among them Atlantic City in 1854, Somers Point in 1886 and Ventnor City in 1903.

What remains is spread out. The seat of government is in Bargaintown, and the township includes Cardiff, English Creek, Farmington, Scullville, Steelmanville and West Atlantic City, plus part of McKee City. West Atlantic City and Anchorage Poynte are not contiguous with the main body. A listing should name the section, because buyers search by those names.

How do the Pinelands rules affect a house here?

The township is one of 56 South Jersey municipalities in the Pinelands National Reserve, and part of it lies in the state-designated Pinelands Area. The Pinelands Commission classed Egg Harbor Township, Hamilton and Galloway as Regional Growth Areas, which pushed residential building here so that trees in the preserved Pine Barrens stay standing.

  • In 2007 the planning board approved 667 homes in the Farmington section: townhouses, homes for buyers 55 and older, and single-family houses.
  • If your lot sits near wetlands or protected land, ask the township's construction office about limits before planning a deck, shed or addition.
  • Wildlife management areas including Malibu Beach, Pork Island and Lester G. MacNamara are public land in the south and east.

What does the township offer commuters and families?

The Atlantic City Expressway crosses the township for 5.3 miles and meets the Garden State Parkway at Interchange 7, which is Parkway Interchange 38. The Parkway runs 8.6 miles through, and Routes 40, 322 and 9 plus county routes 559, 563, 575 and 585 carry local traffic. NJ Transit buses 502, 507, 508 and 509 link the township with Atlantic City. Most of Atlantic City International Airport lies in the northern part of the township. The Census puts mean travel to work at 23.3 minutes, the shortest of the four towns.

The township has 297 miles of roads, 207 of them municipal. Harbor Square, the former Shore Mall, is the regional shopping center, and the Atlantic County Bikeway runs 7.5 miles from the mall toward Hamilton Township.

What draws buyers to the township besides the price?

  • Malibu Beach Wildlife Management Area covers 95.7 acres of marsh, dunes and back-bay shoreline and is known locally as Dog Beach, one of the few New Jersey beaches that permits dogs.
  • Storybook Land, a 20 acre children's park, opened in 1955 on the township's mainland side.
  • The township was one of the first five in the state, in 2017, to authorize medical cannabis dispensaries.
  • The township borders Ocean City and has Great Egg Harbor Bay shoreline in its eastern segment.

Name the nearest of these in your listing, since they are what a buyer from outside Atlantic County will recognize.

Which schools serve Egg Harbor Township homes?

Egg Harbor Township Schools run seven schools for pre-kindergarten through grade 12. The 2023-24 enrollment was 7,473 students with a 10.9 to 1 student-teacher ratio. Davenport and Swift-Slaybaugh serve the early grades, the Dr. Joyanne D. Miller school takes grades 4 and 5, Alder Avenue and Fernwood Avenue are the middle schools, and Egg Harbor Township High School had 2,299 students. Students can also go to the Atlantic County Institute of Technology in Mays Landing or the Charter-Tech High School for the Performing Arts in Somers Point.

What do the state's transfer fees look like for a typical Egg Harbor Township sale?

With a median value of $312,700, most township sales fall in the state's lower schedule for deals up to $350,000.

New Jersey realty transfer fee, standard sale up to $350,000
Price bandRate per $500

$150,000 to $200,000$3.35
$200,000 to $350,000$3.90

Source: NJ Division of Taxation. The state's worked example puts the fee at $1,910 on a $325,000 deed with no exemption. Seniors, blind or disabled sellers and low or moderate income housing qualify for a partial exemption using Form RTF-1.

How do I appeal an assessment or record a deed in Atlantic County?

Atlantic County's Board of Taxation sits in Mays Landing at 5909 Main Street and can be reached at (609) 645-5820. Petitions are due by April 1, and hearings are typically held between April and September at the Historic Courthouse. The board mails a hearing notice at least ten days ahead, and any comparable sales you rely on must reach the board, the municipal assessor and the municipal clerk at least seven days before the hearing. Good comparables are real sales in the same town within the year before the prior October 1; most foreclosures, sheriff's sales, estate sales and short sales are treated as not usable. A reduction comes back as a credit through a revised bill from the tax collector, and you have 45 days from the judgment to go to the State Tax Court.

A resident seller signs GIT/REP-3 for the deed. Nonresidents use GIT/REP-1 or GIT/REP-2 unless a listed assurance applies.

More questions about Egg Harbor, NJ

Is Egg Harbor Township the same as Egg Harbor City?

No. The state lists Egg Harbor Township and Egg Harbor City as separate municipalities. This page covers the township, which had 48,435 residents in the 2025 Census estimate.

Do I need a smoke and CO certificate to sell in Egg Harbor Township?

Yes, a change of ownership calls for a state smoke and carbon monoxide certificate. Ask the township's Bureau of Fire Inspections for its form, fee and timing before you pick a closing date.

What is the median home value in Egg Harbor Township?

The Census Bureau reports $312,700 for owner-occupied homes in the 2020 to 2024 period, and 84.4 percent of homes are owner occupied.

When is the Atlantic County tax appeal deadline?

April 1 of the tax year, filed with the Atlantic County Board of Taxation. Where a revaluation was done, the deadline is May 1.

How long are Atlantic County hearing notices sent in advance?

At least ten days before the hearing. Comparable sales evidence is due to the board, the assessor and the clerk at least seven days before.

Why does the size of Galloway Township, NJ matter to a house seller?

Galloway Township is the largest municipality in New Jersey by area, so two houses with the same Galloway address can sit miles apart and attract very different buyers. Total area is 114.49 square miles, of which 88.67 are land and 25.82 are water.

The Census Bureau estimates 38,380 residents for July 2025, up from 37,813 at the 2020 census. That is a density of only 426.5 people per square mile, compared with 15,469 in Garfield, Bergen County. Galloway serves as a growing edge city to neighboring Atlantic City.

For 2020-2024 the Census Bureau shows 79.8% owner-occupied housing, a median home value of $298,900 and median gross rent of $1,619. Residents aged 65 and over make up 21.6% of the population.

How did Galloway Township develop, and which communities do buyers search?

Galloway began as a royal grant and was later divided into many smaller towns. A royal patent from King George III created the township on April 4, 1774, when it belonged to Gloucester County, and the legislature incorporated it on February 21, 1798. After Atlantic County formed in 1837, pieces were cut away to create Mullica Township, Egg Harbor City, Absecon, Brigantine and Port Republic.

The township now has no single downtown. Census-designated places inside it are Absecon Highlands, Cologne, Germania, Leeds Point, Oceanville, Pomona (7,416 residents in 2020), Smithville (7,242) and the Stockton University campus area. Other place names, including Higbeetown, Pinehurst and Somersville, show up in older deeds.

Galloway borders Absecon, Atlantic City, Egg Harbor City, Egg Harbor Township, Hamilton Township, Mullica Township and Port Republic in Atlantic County, plus Bass River and Washington townships in Burlington County and Little Egg Harbor in Ocean County. A buyer shopping for a Galloway address often compares it with houses in those towns.

What inspection does Galloway Township require when a house is resold?

Galloway requires a fire certificate on every residential resale, covering smoke detectors, carbon monoxide detectors and fire extinguishers only. Township code Chapter 153 says the inspection must happen before the new owners can occupy the dwelling.

The application, inspection and certificate go through the Fire Department at 300 E. Jimmie Leeds Road. The fee depends on how much notice you give, so ask for the inspection as soon as you have a closing date.

Galloway Township fire certificate fees by notice before change of ownership
When the request is receivedFee
More than 10 business days before the change of ownership$45
Four to 10 business days before$90
Fewer than four business days before$161

Violating the ordinance can bring a fine of up to $2,000, up to 90 days in jail or community service, and each day counts as a separate offense. Unlike Freehold Township, Galloway's resale inspection does not cover the rest of the house, since the ordinance limits it to the three fire safety items.

What does Galloway Township ask of an owner who rents out the house?

Rentals follow a separate and fuller inspection than resales. Under Galloway's rental ordinance, a certificate of occupancy is required on any rental, renewed every year or at each new occupant, whichever comes first, at $50 per inspection.

  • The lease must accompany the application and list every occupant's name and age.
  • Smoke and carbon monoxide detectors are required in every rental unit.
  • A detached one- or two-family rental needs a fire extinguisher of at least 2A:10B:C and at most 10 pounds, mounted within 10 feet of the kitchen with its top no higher than five feet from the floor.
  • A rental with a fireplace needs a chimney certification and proof that the dryer vent has been cleaned, or a notarized letter from the owner.
  • More than two follow-up inspections trigger another $50 fee.

The Housing Department handles applications at (609) 652-3700, extensions 241 or 249. Inspection requests themselves must now be emailed to the Construction office at inspect@gtnj.org with the permit number, address, type of inspection and your phone number.

How do the Pinelands and past storms affect a Galloway Township house?

Much of Galloway lies inside a protected landscape, and some parcels carry extra rules. The township is one of 56 South Jersey municipalities in the Pinelands National Reserve, a 1.1 million acre area Congress established in 1978, and parts of Galloway also fall in the state-designated Pinelands Area. Ask the Community Development office whether your parcel is in that area before you promise a buyer an addition or a new outbuilding.

Weather history is part of the picture too. In spring 2007 gypsy moth caterpillars defoliated a large swath of oak and other hardwoods in the township, and the township did not apply for state spraying that year. Tropical Storm Irene made its second U.S. landfall at Brigantine on August 28, 2011, next to Galloway.

The Community Development Department says the homeowner, not the contractor, is responsible for obtaining a permit. Residential contractors need a state Consumer Affairs 13VH number, so keep contractor names and permit numbers for any work you did before selling.

What do nonresident and out-of-state owners owe on a Galloway Township sale?

A nonresident seller prepays estimated gross income tax at the closing table. The state's formula multiplies the gain by 10.75%, but the payment can never be below 2% of the consideration written in the deed, even if there is no gain.

On a $300,000 deed, the floor works out to $6,000. The payment goes with the deed and the GIT/REP-1 form to the Atlantic County Clerk, who forwards it to the state. A seller who wants to avoid delays can prepay at a Division of Taxation regional office and receive a stamped GIT/REP-2 before closing.

  • A New Jersey resident signs the GIT/REP-3 instead and pays nothing up front.
  • A nonresident can still use the GIT/REP-3 if one of its listed assurances fits, such as a deed for $1,000 or less or a settlement with no net proceeds to the seller.
  • Selling a principal residence that qualifies under Internal Revenue Code section 121 is another listed assurance, when the entire gain can be excluded.

The Division of Taxation's GIT/REP Unit answers questions at 609-322-9275, and the Division suggests contacting it at least two weeks before a complicated closing.

How do schools, the Parkway and Stockton University influence Galloway Township buyers?

Buyers care about the Garden State Parkway and the schools. The Parkway runs 5.7 miles through the township, with Interchange 40 for U.S. Route 30, Interchange 41 for Jimmie Leeds Road and Interchange 44 for Pomona. Route 50 and County Routes 561, 563 and 575 also cross the township, and NJ Transit buses 508, 554 and 559 reach Atlantic City. The mean commute is 23.6 minutes.

Galloway Township Public Schools serve pre-K through grade 8 in six schools, with 3,164 students in 2021-22. High school students attend Absegami High School, in the township, as part of the Greater Egg Harbor Regional High School District, and families in the western part may choose Cedar Creek High School in Egg Harbor City.

Stockton University sits in the Pomona section, and Atlantic Cape Community College, with campuses in Mays Landing, Atlantic City and Cape May Court House, serves the county. A house bought as a rental brings the inspection rules above into play.

More questions about Galloway, NJ

Does Galloway Township require an inspection to sell a house?

Yes, a fire certificate. Galloway requires an inspection of smoke detectors, carbon monoxide detectors and fire extinguishers on every residential resale, and it must be done before the new owners occupy the home.

What does the Galloway Township resale fire certificate cost?

It costs $45 when the request arrives more than 10 business days before the change of ownership, $90 for four to 10 business days, and $161 for fewer than four business days.

Where do I apply for the Galloway Township fire certificate?

The application, inspection and certificate are handled by the Fire Department at 300 E. Jimmie Leeds Road. The township's Housing Department can be reached at (609) 652-3700, extensions 241 or 249.

How much tax does a nonresident owe when selling in Galloway Township?

At least 2% of the deed consideration is prepaid at closing as estimated New Jersey gross income tax. The actual figure can be higher, since the formula uses the gain times 10.75%, and the seller can claim a refund after filing a nonresident return.

Is Galloway Township in the Pinelands?

Yes, in part. Galloway is within the Pinelands National Reserve, and parts of it are in the state-designated Pinelands Area. Ask the township's Community Development office about your specific parcel.

What speeds up a house sale in Hamilton Township, Atlantic County?

Three things set the pace here: a resale inspection arranged through the township, a clear tax payoff and a deed recorded at the courthouse in Mays Landing. This page covers the Atlantic County township around Mays Landing, a different place from the Hamilton near Trenton.

The Census Bureau estimates 28,845 residents for July 1, 2025, up 5.0 percent from its 2020 base. Owners live in 70.7 percent of homes, and the typical owner-occupied value is $246,200. Listings range from suburban streets in the developed east to rural lots in the pine forest of the west, and a cash buyer who takes the house as it stands removes loan approval and repair negotiations from that timeline.

What sets Hamilton Township apart from other Atlantic County towns?

Hamilton Township has the most land of any municipality in New Jersey at 110.90 square miles, and it calls itself the state's largest municipality. Counting water as well, only Galloway Township is bigger. Mays Landing, the Atlantic County seat since the county formed in 1837, sits inside the township with the census-designated places of McKee City and Mizpah.

A great deal of that land is protected. The township belongs to the New Jersey Pinelands National Reserve, and the Pinelands Commission regulates the western three-quarters, which remains pine forest. The eastern quarter is a Regional Growth Area where development is allowed and encouraged, and most residents live there, near the Hamilton Mall and other shopping centers.

  • Mays Landing: 5,603 residents in 2020, home to the county courthouse complex.
  • McKee City: 9,758 residents in 2020, the largest census-designated place in the township.
  • Lake Lenape and the Great Egg Harbor River: recreation areas, with the Lake Lenape parks covering over 2,000 acres.

If the house sits on or near undeveloped land, ask the township planning and zoning office whether the parcel lies inside the Pinelands Area before you describe what a buyer could add or build.

How did Hamilton Township grow into what it is now?

The township was incorporated on February 5, 1813, from parts of Egg Harbor and Weymouth townships. Its early economy followed the Great Egg Harbor River: a shipyard and trading post opened near Babcock Creek at Mays Landing in 1756, and more than 200 vessels were built along the river between 1830 and 1880.

The population stood at 6,017 in 1960, 16,012 in 1990 and 27,484 in 2020. Retail is part of the economy, with more than 3,000,000 square feet of stores including Hamilton Mall, Consumer Square and Hamilton Commons, and a winery on a 57-acre vineyard.

Which Hamilton Township figures should guide my asking price?

The average home here was billed $5,931 in 2025, on a general rate of 3.520 per $100. The table sets the state and Census numbers side by side.

The state's effective rate for the township is 2.179, the general rate adjusted for how assessments compare with market value. Average sales ran about $144,000 above the average assessment, so lean on recent sales when you set the price.

What inspection happens before a Hamilton Township resale?

Township fire inspectors check smoke and carbon monoxide detectors before a house is resold or reoccupied, and requests go through the online title transfer inspection portal linked from the Fire Prevention page. The state Uniform Fire Code requires a smoke alarm certificate for one-family and two-family houses that are sold, leased or reoccupied, and only the municipality issues it.

The construction office at the township hall, 6101 Thirteenth Street in Mays Landing, schedules its own inspections in person or by fax and does not accept phoned-in requests. A certificate stays valid for six months, so ask for the inspection once you have a contract and a closing date.

  • Working smoke alarms on each floor, the basement included, and near sleeping areas.
  • A carbon monoxide alarm where the code calls for one.
  • Sealed ten-year smoke alarms when you replace old ones.

Code Enforcement also responds to property maintenance complaints, so clear any open issue before you list.

How do assessments and appeals work in Hamilton Township?

Appeals go to the Atlantic County Board of Taxation at 5909 Main Street in Mays Landing. A petition must arrive before the close of business at 4 p.m. on April 1, because a postmark does not count, and petitions about added or omitted assessments follow the same rule on December 1. The 2026 April deadline has passed.

The board accepts filings online through MyNJAppeal.com, where evidence can be uploaded until seven days before the hearing. Assessment cards usually arrive in late January, and the board publishes lists of usable comparable sales. The test is whether your assessment exceeds what the house would sell for.

Request a payoff figure from the township tax collector before closing, and check the parcel in the county's property assessment search before you set a price.

What will a Hamilton Township seller pay, and where is the deed filed?

The state's Realty Transfer Fee falls on the seller at recording. The state's own example for a $325,000 deed is $1,910, and the township's average 2025 sale of about $312,000 sits in the same bracket, with a rate that begins at $2.00 per $500.

The Atlantic County Clerk records deeds at the Historic Court House Complex, 5901 Main Street in Mays Landing, which lies inside the township. A satellite office serves Atlantic City at 1333 Atlantic Avenue. Make recording and transfer fee checks out to the Atlantic County Clerk's Office, and send any nonresident Gross Income Tax prepayment to the State of New Jersey Division of Taxation.

  • GIT/REP-3 residency certification for New Jersey residents.
  • Gross Income Tax prepayment for nonresident sellers, set at 2 percent of the price or more.
  • A deed prepared by the closing attorney or title company.

Which schools, highways and buses serve Hamilton Township buyers?

Hamilton Township Schools teach prekindergarten through eighth grade in three schools: Shaner Memorial, the George Hess Educational Complex and William Davies Middle School. Older students attend Oakcrest High School in the township, part of the Greater Egg Harbor Regional High School District. Atlantic Cape Community College's Mays Landing campus has operated since 1968.

A 14-mile stretch of the Atlantic City Expressway crosses the township with three interchanges, and U.S. Routes 40 and 322 and Route 50 cover other directions. NJ Transit buses 502 and 553 reach Atlantic City, and the 315 runs between Cape May and Philadelphia.

More questions about Hamilton (Atlantic), NJ

Is an inspection mandatory before selling in Hamilton Township, Atlantic County?

Yes. Township fire inspectors check smoke and carbon monoxide detectors before resale, and requests go through the online title transfer inspection portal. State law requires the certificate for one-family and two-family houses.

Where does a Hamilton Township deed get recorded?

At the Atlantic County Clerk's Office, 5901 Main Street in Mays Landing, inside the township. A satellite office is at 1333 Atlantic Avenue in Atlantic City.

What is the assessment appeal deadline here?

April 1 at 4 p.m., with December 1 as the date for added or omitted assessments. Filing works online, and a postmark does not satisfy the deadline.

Is this the same Hamilton as the one in Mercer County?

No. They are separate municipalities in different counties, each with its own tax board, clerk and inspection office. This page covers the one around Mays Landing.

Can I sell a house that sits in the Pinelands?

Yes. Pinelands rules govern what can be built, so ask the township planning and zoning office what the parcel's zone allows before you advertise additions or lot splits.
