What should an Evesham Township owner know before selling quickly?

Evesham Township is a large South Jersey suburb in Burlington County, and a quick sale there depends mostly on a short list of local steps: a resale certificate through the fire department, permits for past work, and the state paperwork filed with the deed.

The township covers about 29 square miles and counted 46,826 people in 2020. The Census Bureau estimated 49,525 residents in July 2025, which makes Evesham the most populous municipality in Burlington County. People often say Marlton when they mean Evesham, because Marlton is the best known community inside the township and shares ZIP code 08053 with much of it.

Part of the township sits inside the Pinelands Area, a state-designated zone with its own land use rules. If your lot is near the wooded edge of town, check the zoning map before you describe the property to a buyer, since it affects what a purchaser can add or build later.

How old is Evesham, and why does the history matter to a seller?

Evesham dates to the late 1600s, so many parcels carry old deeds and older houses sit beside postwar subdivisions. Quakers settled the area in 1672, and the township was established in 1688 as Eversham in the Province of West Jersey. It was incorporated again under the 1798 Township Act on February 21, 1798.

The original township was far larger. The population climbed from 4,548 in 1960 to 35,309 in 1990, so a large share of the housing stock went up in a single generation.

Title searches on older parcels can turn up easements or old liens that a closing attorney has to clear before the deed records.

What do Census figures say about Evesham homes and owners?

Evesham is an owner-occupied township with prices above the national median, according to Census QuickFacts. The table below sets the township against the country using the 2020 to 2024 estimates.

Evesham Township against the United States, Census QuickFacts 2020 to 2024 estimates
MeasureEvesham TownshipUnited States
Median value of owner-occupied homes$397,600$332,700
Median gross rent$2,046$1,413
Median household income$118,670$80,734
Residents 65 and older18.9%18.9%
Mean commute in minutes27.826.4

About 89 percent of residents lived in the same house a year earlier, so turnover is modest and a listing that sits unsold tends to stand out. Homes valued near the township median fall in the higher state fee schedule covered further down.

Which roads and transit lines affect an Evesham sale?

Route 70 and Route 73 are the two highways that define the township, and buyers judge a house by how it connects to them. Route 70 crosses the northern part of Evesham from east to west, Route 73 runs along the western border, and County Route 544 (Marlton Parkway and Taunton Lake Road) links the two.

The old Marlton Circle at Routes 70 and 73 once handled about 90,000 vehicles a day and was the site of as many as 175 crashes a year. A grade-separated interchange replaced it in 2011, and the change made commutes toward Philadelphia and Cherry Hill more predictable.

  • NJ Transit bus route 406 runs through the township between Berlin and Philadelphia.
  • The Atco station, just across the border in Waterford Township, carries Atlantic City Line trains to Philadelphia 30th Street and the Atlantic City Rail Terminal.
  • The township reported about 183 miles of roadway in 2010, with the municipality maintaining about 159 of them.

Which schools serve Evesham homes?

Evesham Township School District covers prekindergarten through eighth grade, and Cherokee High School takes students from ninth through twelfth grade. In the 2021 to 2022 school year the local district ran eight schools and enrolled 4,384 students.

The elementary schools named in the district are Beeler, DeMasi, Jaggard, Marlton, Rice and Van Zant, and the two middle schools are DeMasi and Marlton Middle. Cherokee High School had 2,165 students that year after a 210,000 square foot addition opened in 2001.

Families searching for a house usually sort by elementary school zone, so name the school attached to your address in the listing or in any direct conversation with a buyer.

What does Evesham require before a house changes hands?

Evesham directs residential resale certificate requests to the Evesham Township Fire Department, and the fire department's own site, eveshamfire.org, is where inspection scheduling and fees are posted. Start that request early so the certificate is ready when the closing date arrives.

The Community Development office handles permits from the Township Building at 984 Tuckerton Road in Marlton, Room 204, Monday through Friday from 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. The construction office can be reached at 856-983-2914, then option 4. Its published guidance is direct about unpermitted work: a construction permit confirms that work meets fire and building codes, and an insurer can refuse a claim tied to work done without one.

  • Sheds and fences need a zoning permit, and a fence around a pool also needs a building permit meeting the pool barrier code.
  • A homeowners association may need to approve a shed or fence first.
  • Interior sump pump or French drain work needs a construction permit, while exterior-only drainage work does not.
  • Flood zone questions can be checked on the FEMA Flood Map Service Center and the township mapping portal.

If a past owner finished a basement, deck or pool without paperwork, sort that out before you list. A buyer's attorney will ask for permit history, and a gap can stall a sale for weeks.

Can you sell an Evesham rental or short-term rental house?

Yes, but the rental registration and fire inspection records go with the property, so gather them first. Evesham treats short-term rentals such as Airbnb and Vrbo listings like long-term rentals: they must pass a fire department inspection and register with the Township Clerk's Office.

The township requires a Certificate of Smoke Alarm, Carbon Monoxide Alarm, and Portable Fire Extinguisher Compliance each time a new tenant occupies the property, under N.J.A.C. 5:70-2.3. Failing to comply carries a $500 penalty, and the fire department sets the fees for the inspection.

If tenants live in the house, a buyer will want the lease, the deposit amount and the last inspection certificate. A cash purchaser who wants the house empty should say so in writing before the contract is signed, so that notice periods can be planned. For landlord and tenant disputes, the township points residents to the Burlington County court system and Legal Services of New Jersey.

What does the seller handle at closing in Evesham?

The seller pays the state Realty Transfer Fee and signs a Gross Income Tax residency form, and both are filed with the deed at the Burlington County Clerk. The Division of Taxation charges the fee per $500 of the price recited in the deed. For a standard sale over $350,000, the band from $200,000 to $550,000 is $4.80 per $500, which is the band a price near Evesham's median home value reaches.

Homes sold above $1 million add a graduated percent fee that the seller owes, starting at 1 percent of the total price. Most Evesham sales fall well under that line.

The Gross Income Tax form for most New Jersey residents is the GIT/REP-3. Burlington County notified filers that any GIT/REP form signed on or after October 1, 2025 must be the current version, and older versions are rejected at recording. Questions go to the state GIT/REP Unit at 609-322-9275. Nonresident sellers owe an estimated payment of at least 2 percent of the price unless an exemption applies.

The Burlington County Clerk also runs a free Property Fraud Alert system that alerts owners when a document is recorded in their name, and it is worth joining before and after a sale.

How does a fast as-is sale in Evesham usually move?

A fast sale follows a short sequence, and each step has a clear owner. The steps below assume you have clear title and no open permits.

  • Gather the deed, the last tax bill, any rental registration and your mortgage payoff figure.
  • Request the fire department resale certificate and fix anything it flags, or agree in the contract who fixes it.
  • Have your closing attorney order the title search and prepare the deed with the RTF and GIT/REP filings.
  • Close, hand over keys, and let the attorney record the deed with the Burlington County Clerk.

Cash buyers often agree to take a house in its current condition, which removes repair negotiations but not the certificate or the state filings. Ask any buyer to put the price, the closing date and who pays for each inspection in one written document before you commit.

More questions about Evesham, NJ

Do I need a certificate from the township to sell my house in Evesham?

Yes, residential resales go through the Evesham Township Fire Department for a certificate. The township construction pages send resale and rental requests there, and eveshamfire.org lists scheduling and fees. Ask for the inspection date as soon as you decide to sell.

What happens if work on my Evesham house was done without a permit?

A buyer's attorney will likely require it to be resolved before closing. The township says a construction permit confirms work meets fire and building codes, and an insurer may deny a claim tied to unpermitted work. Call the construction office at 856-983-2914, option 4, to learn what a retroactive permit needs.

Who pays the realty transfer fee in an Evesham sale?

The seller pays it. The state charges it when the deed is recorded with the Burlington County Clerk, based on the price in the deed, and an extra graduated fee applies above $1 million. Your closing attorney or title company will calculate the exact figure.

Can I sell a house in Evesham if I live out of state?

Yes. A nonresident seller files a GIT/REP form and pays an estimated Gross Income Tax of at least 2 percent of the price at closing unless an exemption on the form applies. The payment can be claimed back against the final tax owed when you file.

Is part of Evesham in the Pinelands?

Yes, a portion of the township lies in the state-designated Pinelands Area, and the township zoning map and Pinelands Commission maps show which lots are covered. Check your parcel before marketing the property, since Pinelands rules may affect additions or new structures.

Cherry Hill at a glance

Selling in Cherry Hill?

What sets a Cherry Hill home sale apart from a typical New Jersey closing?

Cherry Hill sellers face two separate township inspections before closing, one covering the property's exterior and one covering smoke and carbon monoxide alarms, and each is booked through a different office. Booking both early keeps the closing date from slipping.

The township is large, mostly owner-occupied and built largely in the decades after World War II, so the typical seller owns a single-family house on a suburban lot with trees, fences, driveways and sidewalks that the township cares about. This page walks through the inspections, the tax calendar, the county recording charges and a worked transfer-fee example so you can set a realistic closing date.

How big is Cherry Hill and how did it develop?

Cherry Hill covers about 24 square miles of Camden County, which makes it the county's most populous municipality. It began as Delaware Township in 1844, and in 1961 took the Cherry Hill name from a local farm. Quaker settlers arrived in the late 1600s, the first small cluster was Colestown, and 19th-century farms supplied produce to the Campbell's soup plant across the river in Camden. Growth then jumped after World War II, from about 10,400 residents in 1950 to 31,500 in 1960 and 64,400 in 1970.

Its neighborhoods include Ashland, Barclay, Erlton, Greentree, Kingston Estates, Springdale, Woodcrest and the area around Cherry Hill Mall. Pennsauken Creek marks the eastern line with Burlington County, the Cooper River runs along the southern border beside Route 70, and Haddonfield, Collingswood and Voorhees sit across those lines.

Cherry Hill households and money, Census Bureau estimates
MeasureCherry Hill
Residents, mid-2025 estimate79,965
Homes lived in by their owners76.5%

With three of every four homes owner-occupied and a middle value near $386,000, the typical listing is a family house where condition, curb appeal and school zone matter more than rental income.

Which roads, transit lines and schools matter to Cherry Hill buyers?

Cherry Hill is built around highway access to Philadelphia. Interstate 295 has three exits in the township, including exit 31, which leads directly to the Woodcrest PATCO station, and Routes 38, 41, 70 and 154 cross it. Township roads total about 309 miles, of which the township itself maintains roughly 247. NJ Transit buses reach Philadelphia on the 317, 404 and 406 routes, and the Atlantic City Line stops at the Cherry Hill station.

Schools are the other big talking point. Cherry Hill Public Schools operates 19 schools with about 10,800 students in the 2023 to 2024 school year, including two traditional high schools, Cherry Hill High School East and Cherry Hill High School West, three middle schools and 12 elementary schools. Private options include Camden Catholic High School and the King's Christian School.

  • Mention the PATCO station and I-295 exits in your listing if you are close to them.
  • Name the elementary school zone, since buyers search by it.
  • Note any Cooper River or creek frontage and have the drainage history ready.

What are the two Cherry Hill inspections before closing?

A seller here needs a Certificate of Continued Occupancy from the township and a smoke alarm and carbon monoxide compliance certificate from the fire department. A single-family sale cannot reach closing without them, and they are separate appointments with separate costs.

The occupancy certificate comes from Community Development, which handles property maintenance, at 820 Mercer Street, Room 202. The property maintenance officer looks at exterior areas only. The township lists these items:

  • Sidewalks, driveways and fences.
  • Trees and natural growth.
  • Sanitation and exhaust vents.
  • Grading and drainage, including where sump pumps discharge.
  • Accessory structures and ground surface hazards.

The inspection costs $100, payable ahead of the visit, and you can apply online, in person or by mail. Online applications need office approval before a payment request is emailed, cancellations after payment are not refunded, and the property maintenance line is 856-834-3364. Some condominiums and townhomes are excluded, and the township posts a list of properties that skip the inspection.

The fire department certificate is a different step. It is required for one- and two-family homes before settlement, and sellers are asked to request the appointment three to four weeks early. If the home passes and payment is made, the certificate is handed over at the visit; temporary certificates are not issued, and fire extinguishers are no longer required. The fire department's inspection line is (856) 429-7441. Because the two appointments run on separate calendars, book both the week the contract is signed.

Does the township help with move-out trash after a Cherry Hill sale?

Yes, Cherry Hill offers a one-time courtesy collection for house clean-outs after a sale, covering furniture, carpets, bedding and similar household items. Proof that you applied for a Continued Certificate of Occupancy is required before Public Works will schedule it, pickups happen on Fridays, and the number to call is 856-424-4422.

The same guidelines say no trash or recycling service goes to dwellings under construction, vacant lots or properties lacking a valid certificate of occupancy, so a vacant house waiting on its paperwork may go without pickup. Plan the clean-out around the certificate date, and keep contractor debris out of the cart, because construction waste generated by a contractor has to be hauled away by that contractor.

When are Cherry Hill property taxes due and who collects them?

The four installments land on the first of August, November, February and May, and a ten-day grace period rolls forward to the next business day if it ends on a weekend or holiday. The township mails two bills a year: July covers the third and fourth installments, and January covers the first and second. Money has to be in the tax office by the last grace day, because postmarks do not count.

Late payments accrue 8 percent a year up to $1,500 of arrears and 18 percent on any amount beyond that, running from the original due date. The tax collector also bills sewer rent: residential sewer is a flat annual fee due April 1, with a 10 percent discount for owners 60 or older who live in the property. Ask the tax office at 856-488-7880 for a closing figure that includes any sewer balance. The office gathers money for the school district, the fire district and Camden County along with the township, so the bill you pay includes those shares.

Appeals follow state deadlines, April 1 or May 1 after a revaluation, and go to the Camden County Board of Taxation.

How much is the transfer fee and where does the deed get filed?

The Camden County Clerk files the deed, and the seller owes the state realty transfer fee when it is filed. Above $350,000 the state schedule runs $2.90 per $500 for the first $150,000, $4.25 per $500 for the slice from $150,000 to $200,000 and $4.80 per $500 for the slice from $200,000 to $550,000. On a $400,000 price, those slices add up to about $3,215: $870, then $425, then $1,920. Confirm the figure with your closing attorney, since senior, disabled and low-income rates run lower.

The county's recording schedule lists $30 for page one of a deed, $10 for every added page, a $10 abstracting fee and a $5 homeless trust fund charge, with a $55 floor. Camden County's online land records start in 1978, and the clerk's office answers at 856-225-5300. A New Jersey resident signs a residency certification at closing, while a seller who is leaving the state prepays estimated income tax, so tell your attorney early if you are relocating.

More questions about Cherry Hill, NJ

Are inspections required to sell in Cherry Hill?

Yes, two of them. The township requires a Certificate of Continued Occupancy for single-family resale, and the fire department requires a smoke alarm and carbon monoxide compliance certificate before settlement.

What does the Cherry Hill resale inspection cost?

The occupancy inspection is $100, paid before the inspector arrives. The fire department sets its own charges, which are posted on its checklist.

How early should the Cherry Hill fire inspection be scheduled?

Three to four weeks before settlement. The certificate is given at the appointment if the home complies and payment is made, and temporary certificates are not available.

What are the Cherry Hill tax installment dates?

August 1, November 1, February 1 and May 1. A ten-day grace period applies, and the money must reach the tax office by then because postmarks do not count.

Who files a Cherry Hill deed?

The Camden County Clerk. The posted schedule lists $30 for page one of a deed, $10 for each added page, a $10 abstracting fee and a $5 homeless trust fund charge.

Neighbors in Camden County are Hi-Nella, Lindenwold, Magnolia, Pine Hill, Runnemede, Somerdale, Stratford and Winslow Township, and across the line in Gloucester County are Deptford Township and Washington Township.   • Blackwood and Glendora: census-designated places with 4,622 and 4,784 residents in 2020.
  • Erial: an unincorporated community that is home to Timber Creek Regional High School.
  • The Atlantic City Expressway corridor, which crosses the southwest part of the township.

State data for 2025 put the average residential tax bill here at $7,920, while the 710 homes sold in the state's study averaged $338,576. The table collects those numbers with the Census Bureau's.

Who issues the smoke and carbon monoxide certificate in Gloucester Township?

The fire district serving your street handles it, because the township is split into several fire districts. Fire District No. 4's Bureau of Fire Prevention posts a smoke and carbon monoxide certification application and takes inspection requests by phone or email.

To find your district, search your street address in the township's property tax lookup and read the Special Taxing Districts line on the record. FIRE DISTRICT=F04 means District No. 4. State rules call for the certificate before a one-family or two-family house is sold, and it stays valid for six months from issue, so schedule the inspection close to closing.

The district says alarm requirements can vary with a property's age and layout, and a failed inspection brings a list of fixes and a re-inspection. Ask the township construction office whether any other resale paperwork applies before you list.

How does the Gloucester Township tax office handle a sale?

Quarterly installments come due on the first of February, May, August and November, with the maximum 10-day grace period state law allows. Delinquencies accrue 8 percent a year up to $1,500 and 18 percent beyond that, and the office adds a 6 percent penalty to a balance over $10,000 left open at year end. Current-year taxes still delinquent after November 11 face tax sale before December 30, and payments in that period require cash or certified funds.

The office lists two $250 deductions, one for qualifying seniors and disabled residents and one for veterans. A delay in the tax levy certification stretched the third-quarter 2026 grace period to September 2, 2026, which shows how bill dates can move, so ask for a written payoff figure before closing.

To contest an assessment, file with the Camden County Board of Taxation by 4:00 p.m. on April 1, or May 1 in a town that has done a revaluation. An assessment between $150,000 and $500,000 carries a $25 fee, which covers the township's average residential assessment. Keep paying while the appeal is pending, because skipped payments can get it dismissed.

What will a Gloucester Township seller pay at closing?

The payoff and the state's Realty Transfer Fee are usually the largest items. At or below $350,000 the schedule starts at $2.00 per $500 on the first $150,000, and the state's own worked example puts the fee on a $325,000 deed at $1,910. The seller pays it when the deed is recorded.

  • Payoff of the mortgage, credit line or tax lien.
  • Certificate fee charged by the fire district.
  • The GIT/REP-3 residency certification attached to the deed.

The Camden County Clerk at 520 Market Street in Camden records deeds and accepts electronic recording. Out-of-state sellers prepay Gross Income Tax of 2 percent of the price or more unless an assurance on the GIT/REP-3 applies.

Which schools, roads and buses serve Gloucester Township?

Gloucester Township Public Schools teach prekindergarten through eighth grade in eight elementary schools and three middle schools: Glen Landing, Charles W. Lewis and Ann A. Mullen. Ninth through twelfth graders attend Highland Regional in Blackwood, Timber Creek Regional in Erial or Triton Regional in Runnemede, assigned by address within the Black Horse Pike Regional School District.

In 2010 the township listed 239.44 miles of road, 186.25 of them municipal. The Atlantic City Expressway crosses the southwest corner, Routes 42 and 168 run through the west, and County Routes 534 and 544 cover the center and the northern edge. NJ Transit's 400 bus reaches Philadelphia, and the 403 and 459 serve local trips.

What should a landlord check before selling in Gloucester Township?

The township's downloads page carries a Landlord Identity Registration form, so a rental owner should confirm the registration is current before listing. About 27 percent of homes are renter-occupied and typical rent is $1,592, which makes tenant-occupied houses a normal part of the market. The fire certificate also applies to a lease or change of occupancy.

Does Gloucester Township require a resale certificate of occupancy?

The required certificate is the smoke and carbon monoxide one, issued through the fire district for your address. Ask the township construction office whether any other resale paperwork applies to your house.

How can I tell which fire district my house is in?

Search your street address in the township's property tax lookup and read the Special Taxing Districts line. F04 means Fire District No. 4.

What are the Gloucester Township tax due dates?

The first of February, May, August and November, each with a 10-day grace period. Late balances accrue interest, and taxes still delinquent after November 11 can go to tax sale.

By when must I appeal a Gloucester Township assessment?

By 4:00 p.m. on April 1, or May 1 where the town did a revaluation or reassessment. The Camden County Board of Taxation hears appeals at 509 Lakeland Road in Blackwood and offers a summary hearing with no appearance.

May I sell a Gloucester Township house with liens or a foreclosure pending?

Yes, if the sale price covers every payoff. Get written figures from each lender and from the tax collector, since tax sale charges add fees beyond the posted tax total.

What should I know before selling a house in Belleville?

Belleville is a compact Essex County township of 3.30 square miles of land, and a sale there runs through a township resale certificate, the Essex County Register of Deeds and, for landlords, the township's rent leveling rules. About 56% of homes are owner-occupied, so you will meet both owner-occupant and investor buyers.

The township posts its sale-related forms in one place, which makes it easy to line up paperwork before you list. This page explains those forms, the local numbers and the county and state steps that follow a contract.

How big is Belleville and what do its housing figures show?

Belleville had 38,222 residents in the 2020 census, up from 35,926 in 2010, and the Census Bureau estimates 38,997 for mid-2025. Packed into just over three square miles, that works out to 11,596.5 people per square mile.

Belleville Township housing and household snapshot, Census Bureau QuickFacts (2020-2024 survey period unless noted)

The median value of $421,000 and the 2.65 persons per household point to a market of one- and two-family houses on small lots. Ask an agent for sold prices on your own block instead of relying on the township median.

What is Belleville's history and where does it sit in Essex County?

Belleville grew from a settlement called Second River, renamed Belleville in 1797, and it was incorporated as a township in 1839 from part of Bloomfield. The township reincorporated as a town in 1910 and voted to become a township again in 1981. Congress passed a resolution in 1994 recognizing Belleville as the birthplace of the Industrial Revolution in the United States.

The township borders Bloomfield, Newark and Nutley in Essex County, Lyndhurst and North Arlington in Bergen County, and Kearny in Hudson County. The Second River forms much of the border with Newark through Branch Brook Park, and Belleville calls itself the Cherry Blossom Capital of America because of the park's spring display. Silver Lake, split between Belleville and Bloomfield, is the best-known unincorporated community, alongside Belwood, Big Tree and Soho.

The local economy is also worth a line in a listing. Census figures show 68.5% of residents aged 16 and over in the civilian labor force for 2020-2024, retail sales of about $381 million in 2022 and a per capita retail figure of $10,163. Belleville Township spans only 3.37 square miles in total, so most blocks are within a short walk of a bus line or a commercial street.

Which roads, transit and schools help Belleville sell?

Route 7, Route 21 and County Route 506 pass through Belleville, and the Belleville Turnpike Bridge, also called the Rutgers Street Bridge, crosses the Passaic River to North Arlington. The Silver Lake station provides Newark Light Rail service to Newark Penn Station, and NJ Transit buses 13, 27, 72, 74, 90, 92, 93 and 94 run to Newark. The census puts average commute time at 32.4 minutes.

The Belleville School District has 10 schools and 5,095 students in 2023-24, according to Wikipedia's summary of federal data. The township's own links also point residents to Clara Maass Medical Center, and census figures show health care and social assistance receipts of about $807 million in 2022, the largest business total reported for the township.

  • Transit-minded buyers focus on the Silver Lake light rail station and the Newark bus lines.
  • Drivers focus on Routes 7 and 21 and the Turnpike Bridge crossing.
  • Families ask about the Belleville School District, so name it in your listing.

What does the township require before a sale in Belleville?

Belleville posts a Residential Resale Certificate Application and a separate Commercial Resale Certificate application under its Department of Community Development. Ask that office which form fits your property and whether an inspection must happen before you sign a contract.

The same forms page covers other items that come up around a sale, so read through it before you list.

  • Residential Rental Property / New Tenant Certificate Application, plus a Rent Roster form for landlords.
  • Vacant / Abandoned Property Registration, which applies if the house is empty.
  • Request for List of Owners within 200 Feet, used for planning board and zoning board applications.
  • Zoning Permit Application, Fence Permit Application and Pool Permits, which show what work was approved.
  • Landlord Identity Registration Form, filed with the Township Clerk.
  • Fire Department items such as the Fire Safety Permit, a Home Fire Protection Plan and a Fire Safety Checklist for Homeowners and Renters.

Gather the permit paperwork for any work you finished in the house, including fences, pools and driveways, since the township keeps separate applications for each. Having those approvals ready lets a buyer's attorney confirm the work was permitted without waiting on township offices.

How do rent leveling and landlord rules affect a Belleville sale?

Belleville has a Rent Leveling Board, and its forms include a Vacancy Decontrol Application and a Rent Leveling Complaint Form. If you own a rental, check with the board about registration, any open complaints and whether a vacancy decontrol filing is on file before a buyer's attorney asks.

Buyers of tenant-occupied buildings will want copies of leases and the rent roster, so organize them before you list. The township also posts a Continued Certificate of Occupancy form for short-term rentals, which matters if the house was ever rented that way. A clean file shortens attorney review and reduces last-minute price talks.

What property tax and relief records should I gather in Belleville?

Belleville's Tax Assessor page carries a Property Assessment form and a Guide to Appeal Hearings, and the Tax Collector page carries the PD-5 Senior Property Tax Deduction form, a Veteran's Property Tax Credit form and an online payment portal. The township also links the Essex County Board of Taxation and the state's Property Tax Relief Program.

Pull your latest tax bill and any open balance before you list, because buyers and title companies ask for them. If you have a PD-5 deduction or veteran's credit, the buyer will not inherit it automatically, so ask the Tax Collector whether those benefits change after a sale. The township website also lists a Home Improvement Program with an application and a contractor application, which a buyer planning repairs can read.

Where is the deed recorded and what fees apply at closing?

The Essex County Register of Deeds and Mortgages records the deed, and the Essex County Clerk's site directs callers to the register at 973-621-4960. The seller pays the New Jersey realty transfer fee, and for a deal above $350,000 the state schedule charges $4.80 per $500 on the slice between $200,000 and $550,000.

Some transfers are exempt, including a deed from an executor or administrator to an heir under a will or intestacy and a deed recorded within 90 days of a divorce decree. An estate selling a Belleville house files the state's GIT/REP form according to the estate's residency, and the executor signs it. Ask the title company which forms your closing needs.

More questions about Belleville, NJ

Does Belleville require a resale certificate?

The township posts a Residential Resale Certificate Application and a Commercial Resale Certificate application. Ask the Department of Community Development which one applies and when the inspection must occur.

Where is a Belleville deed recorded?

The Essex County Register of Deeds and Mortgages records it. The county clerk's website lists 973-621-4960 for recording a deed, mortgage or lien.

Does Belleville have rent control?

It has a Rent Leveling Board, with a Vacancy Decontrol Application and a complaint form on the township website. Landlords should confirm their status before selling.

Is a deed from an estate to an heir subject to the realty transfer fee?

No. The state exempts a deed from an executor or administrator to a devisee or heir who receives the property under the will or intestacy. A sale of an estate house to a third party is a normal taxable sale.

How many people live in Belleville?

The Census Bureau estimates 38,997 residents as of July 2025, up from 38,222 in the 2020 census. The township covers 3.30 square miles of land.

What does a quick house sale in Bloomfield, NJ involve?

The fastest Bloomfield sales start with township paperwork already in motion before a buyer appears. A listing, a private sale and a cash purchase all pass through the Township's Transfer of Property Title inspection, and its application is due 30 days before closing.

A listing works for a house that shows well and an owner able to answer repair requests. A cash bid is built for a long punch list, a two- or three-family with tenants, open permits, or an inherited home where the heirs want one closing. About half of Bloomfield's households rent, so many owners are landlords deciding between a sale and one more year of upkeep.

  • Listing with an agent: a broad pool of buyers, a commission, inspections and a lender's calendar.
  • Private sale: nothing owed to a listing agent, but the paperwork is yours.
  • Cash buyer: bought as it stands, a shorter timeline, and a bid reduced by the repairs taken on.

What kind of town is Bloomfield, New Jersey?

Bloomfield packs 56,375 people (Census estimate, July 2025) into 5.34 square miles of land in Essex County, which is 6.2 percent more than in 2020. In 2020 the count was 9,950.3 per square mile. The township borders Belleville, East Orange, Glen Ridge, Montclair, Newark and Nutley in Essex County and Clifton in Passaic County, and it includes the Brookdale and Watsessing neighborhoods plus a slice of Silver Lake.

Owners occupy just 50.7 percent of housing units, which makes Bloomfield a town split evenly between owners and renters. The survey's middle owner-occupied value is $470,800, with household income at $103,604 and rent at $1,824. Of residents, 25.1 percent were born abroad and 30.9 percent are Hispanic or Latino, and 35.0 percent of those 5 and older speak another language at home.

The land was first patented to colonists from Newark and assigned to Essex County in 1675. The Presbyterian Society of Bloomfield formed in 1794, and the township's population jumped from 9,668 in 1900 to 38,077 in 1930, which points to an older housing stock and a long paper trail of permits.

What is the Transfer of Property Title in Bloomfield?

It is the Township's inspection and certificate that every property sale or transfer must pass. The application is due 30 days before the closing date, and the certificate stays valid for six months. The Fire Department handles it from 375 Franklin Street, and the application form says the inspection also serves as the state smoke, carbon monoxide and fire extinguisher certificate.

The form states that the inspection shows only that a general check of the visible parts of the building found no code violations or unsafe conditions at that time. The township's FAQ adds that if a bank insists on a separate certificate, the Fire Prevention Bureau issues one for $35, although state law allows a single certificate.

Bloomfield Transfer of Property Title fees under township code Chapter 149
PropertyFee

Two family dwelling$260

Each additional dwelling unit$60, capped at $2,000 in total

What does the Bloomfield inspector check?

The Township publishes a checklist, and the inspector may ask for more than it lists. Most items are quick repairs, though a few take weeks, such as closing old permits and replacing a lead service line.

  • All construction permits, past and present, closed with final inspections.
  • Proof that any lead or galvanized water service line on private property has been replaced, documented by a New Jersey plumber.
  • A township-approved water meter in place, even if the building is winterized.
  • Sump pumps and downspouts not tied into the sanitary sewer.
  • Smoke and carbon monoxide detectors on each floor and near bedrooms, 10-year sealed battery or hard-wired.
  • A fire-rated, self-closing door between an attached garage and the house.
  • Handrails on stairs with four or more risers, no loose siding or roofing, and numbered units.
  • No unregistered vehicles, debris or trip hazards on the property.

Three-family and larger buildings also need portable fire extinguishers, mounted near an exit within 10 feet of the kitchen. If the new owner will rent the property, the form says the rental must be registered within six months of closing.

Do oil tanks and basement apartments cause problems in Bloomfield?

They can. The township's fire FAQ says an unused oil tank must be removed or abandoned in place within one year, and either path needs a Fire Sub-Code permit from the Building Department. If a tank was removed with a permit, the Fire Department or Building Department may have the paperwork on file, so call the Fire Prevention Bureau before you hunt for records.

Basement apartments are a larger issue. The FAQ states that most are illegal, especially in three-family houses, because they do not meet egress requirements. Check with the Building Inspector before you advertise one as a rental unit, because an unpermitted unit can stall a Transfer of Property Title and spook a lender.

How are Bloomfield property taxes billed and appealed?

Four quarterly installments come due on August 1, November 1, February 1 and May 1, with interest running once ten calendar days have passed. Under N.J.S.A. 54:4-64 a bill that never arrives does not cancel the tax. A new owner or a seller with a lost bill should ask the Tax Collector for the amount due and a duplicate.

The Tax Assessor runs assessments, deductions for senior citizens, disabled persons and veterans, and appeals. Filing closes April 1 of the tax year, and May 1 in a year when a revaluation or reassessment takes effect. State relief programs listed by the township include the Homestead Rebate, NJSAVER, the Property Tax Deduction or Credit and Property Tax Reimbursement, so an owner receiving one should tell the closing attorney.

The Tax Assessor's Office sits at 1 Municipal Plaza, first floor, Room 108. Payments to the Tax Collector can be made online or in person.

What do trains, highways and schools add to Bloomfield listings?

The Garden State Parkway has four interchanges in the township, numbered 148 through 151, with 148 and 151 complete and 149 and 150 partial. The Essex toll plaza sits southbound just south of interchange 150. County Road 506, its spur and County Road 509 also cross the township, and Bloomfield has 95.39 miles of roadway in all.

South Bloomfield is served by two NJ Transit Montclair-Boonton Line stations, one off Bloomfield Avenue downtown and one at Watsessing Avenue and Orange Street. About 55 percent of weekday trains continue to New York Penn Station, and weekend trains end at Hoboken. Mean travel time to work is 32.4 minutes. Bloomfield Public Schools run 11 schools and enrolled 6,191 students in 2021 to 2022, from pre-kindergarten through Bloomfield High School and Bridges Academy. Bloomfield Tech High School is a countywide magnet school.

When should a Bloomfield owner look at a cash bid?

A cash bid deserves a look when the Transfer of Property Title would take longer than you can wait, or when repairs would cost more than the discount. Get in writing from any buyer who orders the inspection, who pays the fee and who replaces a lead service line if one turns up.

For an estate, the state treats an executor's sale to an outside buyer as taxable for the realty transfer fee, while a transfer to a named heir is exempt. Compare what each path nets and let a New Jersey attorney review the contract.

More questions about Bloomfield, NJ

Is a smoke detector certificate separate from the Bloomfield Transfer of Property Title?

Usually not. The township's application form says the Transfer of Property Title inspection also serves as the smoke and carbon monoxide compliance certificate. A separate certificate from the Fire Prevention Bureau costs $35 if your bank refuses the single one.

How long before closing should I apply for a Transfer of Property Title in Bloomfield?

30 days. The township's form says the application must be submitted 30 days prior to the closing date, and the certificate is valid for six months. Reinspection after a failed visit costs $25.

Do I have to replace a lead water line to sell in Bloomfield?

Yes, if the service line on your property is lead or galvanized. The township says the owner must replace it and show proof before a Transfer of Property Title is issued. A plumber from New Jersey must inspect and document the line's material.

By what date must a Bloomfield assessment appeal be filed?

April 1 of the tax year, moving to May 1 in a year when a revaluation or reassessment takes effect. The Tax Assessor's Office has the forms.

Does selling to my own child avoid the New Jersey transfer fee?

Yes, a sale from parent to child is exempt, adopted children included. A stepchild does not qualify, so a parent selling to a stepchild owes the fee unless the child was legally adopted.

Irvington at a glance

How can you sell a house fast in Irvington, New Jersey?

An Irvington owner can hire an agent, sell without one or take a cash offer for the house in its current state. Whichever it is, the township wants a housing inspection before title passes. That requirement drives the timeline, so begin it when you decide to sell.

Fewer than one in three housing units here is owner-occupied, so a good number of sellers are landlords or heirs. The inspection fee scales with the number of dwelling units in the building.

  • Listing: best for a house that will pass inspection with little work and appraise well.
  • Private sale: works if you can manage the inspection, the contract and the buyer's financing without an agent.
  • Cash sale: fits a house with code violations, tenants or probate complications, because the purchase contract can be written around the condition.

Where is Irvington and how did it get its name?

Irvington is a small, dense township of 2.92 square miles in Essex County. Maplewood lies to the west and Newark to the east, with Hillside and Union to the south and southwest. The Elizabeth River runs through it near Civic Square.

Until the middle of the 1800s the place was called Camptown. After a well-known ballad about Camptown races was published in 1850, residents worried about the association and renamed it for the author Washington Irving. It became an incorporated village on March 27, 1874, a town in 1898, and a township after a 1982 referendum.

An amusement park, Olympic Park, straddled the Irvington and Maplewood line from 1887 to 1965. Population rose from 1,677 in 1880 to 56,733 in 1930. It has stayed between about 54,000 and 61,500 since then, reaching 61,176 in the 2020 census and an estimated 62,233 in July 2025.

What do Census figures show about Irvington housing and residents?

Irvington is a rental-heavy township with the lowest home values of the four municipalities in the same Census comparison. QuickFacts shows owners in 29.6 percent of units, with a median owned home worth $335,600.

Rent at the median is $1,386 a month. Owners pay $2,489 with a mortgage and $1,026 without. Across 23,542 households of roughly 2.57 people, median income is $61,609, and 19.0 percent of residents fall below the poverty line.

Foreign-born residents account for 35.5 percent of the population, and 32.4 percent of people aged 5 and up speak another language at home. If several relatives share ownership, a short written summary of key dates in their own language keeps everyone on schedule.

What does the Certificate of Housing Compliance require when you sell in Irvington?

Irvington's code makes it unlawful to sell, convey or transfer a building with residential units, or for a buyer to take title or possession, until a Certificate of Housing Compliance has been issued. The Department of Housing issues it after an application and an inspection. The online portal at irvingtonportal.us handles the application and the separate Fire Department inspection.

Irvington certificates and fees, from the Township Code property maintenance chapter on ecode360
CertificateWhen it appliesFee or term
Certificate of Housing ComplianceSale or transfer of a building with residential units$237 per unit up to three units, $116 per unit beyond three
Temporary certificateViolations that will not be fixed before closingNonrenewable, up to six months
Certificate of HabitabilityRenting a dwelling unit to a new tenant$98 per unit, $47 per reinspection, renewed every two years

For an as-is sale, the contract must be attached to the application and signed by both seller and buyer. If the inspection finds violations that stay unrepaired, the director may issue the temporary certificate, and the buyer then acknowledges the duty to fix them. Liability for skipping the certificate falls on both the owner and the purchaser.

The code's exemption section lists transfers between immediate family members, a property inspected within the prior six months, a purchase made to demolish the building and probate transfers to heirs under a will. Ask the Housing Department how those exemptions apply to your sale. A denied certificate can be appealed in writing to the Business Administrator, who must decide within five business days.

Where do you apply, and who inspects?

The Housing and Building office sits in the Municipal Building, Room 201, at 1 Civic Square. Its page lists an evening housing inspector available Monday to Friday from 5:00 to 9:00 p.m. and Saturday from 9:00 a.m. to 2:00 p.m., which helps working owners schedule around a job.

  • Owners of any building in the township, residential or commercial, must give the Housing Department, Tax Collector and Tax Assessor their true home address and company address.
  • Vacant properties go through the Vacant Property Registration Program, with registration on the township portal.
  • Violation notices become orders if no written petition for a hearing is filed within 10 days, so respond to any notice quickly.
  • Fines under the property maintenance code run from $50 for a first violation to $1,000 for a fourth, which also requires a court appearance.

Of the 69.44 miles of road within the township, Irvington maintains 55.98.

How do roads, buses and schools shape the Irvington housing market?

Irvington sits between Newark and the suburbs, and transit is a selling point. The Garden State Parkway passes through the center of the township with exits 143 and 144. Interstate 78 touches the southeastern edge at Exit 54, and County Road 509 is the main local road.

  • Buses: the Irvington Bus Terminal on Springfield Avenue is one of NJ Transit's busiest. Route 107 reaches the Port Authority Bus Terminal in Midtown, and nine routes run to Newark.
  • Air: Newark Liberty International Airport is in neighboring Newark and Elizabeth.
  • Schools: Irvington Public Schools run pre-kindergarten through grade 12 and are one of 31 former Abbott districts. The district had 12 schools and 8,020 students in 2019-20.
  • Business incentives: parts of the township lie in an Urban Enterprise Zone established in May 1996, which expires in May 2027 and allows a reduced 3.3125 percent sales tax at eligible merchants. The area around the bus terminal became a state-designated transit village in July 2015.

What do taxes, recording and state fees add to an Irvington sale?

Deeds for all 22 Essex County municipalities are recorded by the county Register of Deeds and Mortgages, whose files reach back to 1637. Assessment appeals are filed with the Essex County Board of Taxation on Form A-1, normally by April 1, and the Tax Court hears further appeals filed within 45 days of the board's judgment.

State law puts the Realty Transfer Fee on the seller. Because Irvington's median owned home, $335,600, sits under $350,000, the lower schedule governs, topping out at $3.90 per $500 for the slice between $200,000 and $350,000. A landlord living outside New Jersey files GIT/REP-1 and prepays tax of 2 percent of the price or 8.97 percent of the net gain, unless the form's exemptions apply.

More questions about Irvington, NJ

Do I need a certificate to sell my house in Irvington?

Yes. The Township Code requires a Certificate of Housing Compliance before any building with residential units is sold, conveyed or transferred. The Housing Department issues it after an application and an inspection, and a Fire Department inspection is also required, with both started on the township's online portal.

How much does the Irvington sale inspection cost?

The code sets $237 per dwelling unit up to three units in a building and $116 for each unit above three. A single-family house therefore costs $237 and a three-family $711. Reinspections carry their own fee, so fix the listed items before the first visit and confirm current amounts with the Housing Department.

Can I sell an Irvington house as-is if it has violations?

Yes, with conditions. The as-is contract must be attached to the application and signed by both parties. If violations remain unrepaired at closing, the director may issue a nonrenewable temporary certificate lasting up to six months, and the buyer acknowledges in writing the duty to bring the property into compliance.

Are any Irvington transfers exempt from the certificate?

The code's exemption section lists family transfers, a property inspected within six months before the transfer, a purchase for demolition and probate transfers to heirs under a will. The wording is older than the latest amendments, so ask the Housing Department to confirm in writing that an exemption covers your sale.

Where is the deed recorded for an Irvington sale?

At the Essex County Register of Deeds and Mortgages, which covers the county's 22 municipalities. A title company or attorney typically files the deed together with the transfer fee affidavit and GIT/REP form, so you seldom visit in person.

Sell Your Deptford House for Cash

Tell us about your Deptford house.

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

Deptford at a glance

Selling in Deptford?
We buy Deptford houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.
Get My Cash Offer →

What is the quickest way to sell a house in Deptford?

Deptford owners have three ways out: an agent listing, a private sale, or a straight purchase by a cash buyer. The choice usually follows the condition of the house and the calendar. A tidy house with months to spare suits the open market, while worn systems, tenants, an estate, or a payoff date on the horizon point toward a direct sale.

Deptford Township had an estimated 32,600 residents on July 1, 2025, up from 31,977 at the 2020 count. Delays tend to come from paperwork and repairs, so the sections below cover the township offices, the Gloucester County Clerk, and the state forms that go with every deed.

  • Agent listing: the most exposure, with showings and a buyer who typically needs a mortgage and an appraisal.
  • Private sale: no commission to pay, though pricing, disclosures and the attorney review fall to you.
  • Cash purchase: no showings and no repair list, and the offer reflects the work the buyer inherits.

What should I know about Deptford before I price a house here?

Deptford is a southeastern suburb of Philadelphia, about 10 miles from the city on the New Jersey side of the Walt Whitman Bridge and roughly 50 miles northwest of Atlantic City. Deptford spreads over 17.33 square miles and touches Woodbury, Woodbury Heights, Wenonah, Westville, West Deptford, Washington Township and Mantua Township, with Bellmawr, Runnemede and Gloucester Township across the Camden County line.

The place is old. It was formed in 1695 as Bethlehem and incorporated as a township in 1798. Its best-known story is the 1793 balloon landing at the Clement Oak, the first hot air balloon landing in North America. Most of the housing, though, came with the post-war boom: the population went from about 7,300 in 1950 to nearly 17,900 in 1960 and passed 24,000 by 1970. A lot of the housing stock dates from that boom, which is why roofs, heating systems and wiring draw attention at inspection.

Neighborhood names matter to buyers. Oak Valley, a Census-designated place with about 3,500 residents, lies inside the township, along with the unincorporated communities of Almonesson, Good Intent, Lake Tract, Jericho, Hammond Heights, Westcottville and Woodbury Gardens.

How do Deptford's roads, transit and shopping affect a sale?

Access to Philadelphia is a selling point for Deptford. Routes 41, 42, 45, 47 and 55 all cross the township, and county routes 534, 544, 551 and 553 fill in the grid. The New Jersey Turnpike is reached at Exit 3 in Bellmawr and Runnemede, and a short 0.07-mile piece of Interstate 295 touches the township. NJ Transit buses on the 400, 401, 402, 408, 410 and 412 lines run to Philadelphia, with local service on the 455 and 463.

Deptford Mall, the largest mall in the South Jersey region at about 1.07 million square feet of leasable space, anchors the retail side, with strip malls, restaurants and a movie theater around it. Tall Pines State Preserve, a 111-acre park that opened in November 2015 as Gloucester County's first state park, sits on the border with Mantua Township.

As of 2010 the township had about 150 miles of road: roughly 99 municipal, 29 county, 19 state, and 3.4 under the Turnpike Authority.

Which schools serve Deptford homes?

One district, Deptford Township Schools, covers the whole township and had 3,942 students in 2020-21. The elementary schools are Good Intent, Lake Tract, Oak Valley and Shady Lane for grades 1 to 5, with Central Early Childhood Center and Pine Acres Early Childhood Center covering the youngest grades. Monongahela Middle School takes grades 6 to 8, and Deptford Township High School takes grades 9 to 12.

County students may also apply to the Gloucester County Institute of Technology, a no-tuition technical high school based in Deptford. Ask the district which of the four elementary schools your street feeds and give that answer to buyers early.

How does Deptford compare on income and housing costs?

Survey estimates for 2020 through 2024 show a township where owners live in roughly three of every four homes and a typical owned home is valued at $277,100.

Deptford township. Figures come from Census Bureau QuickFacts: the population row is the July 2025 estimate and the rest are 2020-2024 survey estimates.
MeasureDeptford
Estimated residents32,600
Homes occupied by an owner75.7%
Typical value of an owned home$277,100
Median gross rent$1,661
Households11,916

Commute26.0 minutes on average

Monthly owner costs run $2,112 with a mortgage and $927 without one, while median rent is $1,661. An heir deciding whether to rent out an inherited house can compare those three numbers.

Does the 2021 tornado still matter when I sell?

It can. An EF3 tornado with winds up to 150 miles per hour, produced by the remnants of Hurricane Ida, struck Deptford on September 1, 2021 and damaged more than 100 homes. A repaired house should have closed permits and passed final inspections on file. One that was patched without permits, or left half-fixed, can stall a mortgage buyer at the inspection or appraisal.

If your house had storm repairs, collect the permit numbers, contractor invoices and insurance papers before you list. The township construction office at 1011 Cooper Street answers questions about open permits and final inspections at (856) 845-5300, weekdays from 8:30 until 4:30. A cash buyer can take unfinished work as it stands, and the offer will account for it.

What local approvals does a Deptford sale need?

The township construction office takes applications for a Housing Certificate of Occupancy. Before signing a contract, ask that office whether your sale needs one and what the inspection covers, since the buyer's attorney is likely to raise it.

Landlords have one more item. The township clerk's page cites N.J.S.A. 46:8-28, which requires rental owners to register with the clerk, and warns of fines reaching $500 for owners who skip it. Selling a tenant-occupied house means checking that your registration is current; the Clerk's Office number is 856-686-2203.

What will closing cost a Deptford seller?

The seller owes the state a realty transfer fee, charged on a sliding scale per $500 of price. Applying the schedule to a $277,100 sale, the Census median for owned homes here, produces roughly $1,536. A $350,000 sale comes to about $2,105, and anything above $350,000 uses a higher schedule.

  • Transfer fee: paid by the seller, with an affidavit (form RTF-1) filed whenever an exemption is claimed.
  • Recording: the Gloucester County Clerk adds a $20 indexing fee when a paper deed shows up without its cover sheet.
  • Seller's tax form: a GIT/REP form signed at closing. New Jersey residents sign the GIT/REP-3 residency certification, and nonresident sellers may owe a prepayment of at least 2 percent of the price.
  • Payoffs: mortgages, liens and unpaid municipal charges are subtracted from your proceeds.

A listing agent's commission is whatever your agreement says, so get the figure in writing before you compare a listing with a cash offer.

Where does the deed go after a Deptford closing?

Deptford deeds are filed with the Gloucester County Clerk. The clerk's land records page requires one of the GIT/REP forms with every deed, and the Record Room answers at 856-853-3230. The county also runs a free Property Fraud Alert that notifies you whenever a document is filed under your name, which is worth setting up after a sale or an inheritance.

For a copy of an older deed, the clerk's page points owners to the online land records search, where one can be printed free, and warns about mailers that charge $75 to $86 for the same document.

When is a direct sale the better fit in Deptford?

A direct purchase fits when speed or condition matters more than the final few thousand dollars. In Deptford that might be a parent's house nobody wants to repair, a rental whose tenants are leaving, a property with storm or age damage, or a mortgage slipping behind. Get offers in writing, ask which closing costs the buyer covers, and set the net figure beside your best listing estimate.

More questions about Deptford, NJ

Will a Deptford buyer take a house that needs work?

Yes. A cash buyer takes the property as it stands and prices the work into the offer. A buyer relying on a mortgage may ask for repairs after the inspection or appraisal.

Which office files the deed for a Deptford sale?

The Gloucester County Clerk. The deed has to carry a GIT/REP form, and a paper filing without a cover sheet adds a $20 indexing fee. The Record Room number is 856-853-3230.

What transfer fee would a Deptford seller owe?

It scales with price. On the state schedule, $277,100 produces about $1,536 and $350,000 about $2,105. The seller is responsible for it.

Is there a township inspection before a Deptford sale?

Call the construction office at (856) 845-5300. It handles Housing Certificate of Occupancy applications and can say whether your sale needs one and what gets checked.

Does a rented Deptford house need landlord registration before I sell?

Rental owners register with the township clerk under N.J.S.A. 46:8-28, and the clerk lists fines reaching $500 for skipping it. Make sure yours is current before the buyer's attorney asks.

What should I know before selling fast in East Windsor?

Match the method to your deadline. East Windsor owners can work with an agent, go it alone, or take a cash offer, and the best fit depends on condition, tenants and timing. The township adds a step of its own: a fire prevention check of smoke detectors, carbon monoxide detectors and an extinguisher before a single-family home or condominium is sold.

East Windsor's population was estimated at 30,562 in mid-2025, compared with 30,045 in 2020 and 27,190 in 2010. Owners live in about 61 percent of the homes, and tenants in the rest.

  • Working with an agent: reaches financed buyers, and takes the longest.
  • Going it alone: you handle price, contract and the township check yourself.
  • Cash sale as-is: helps with postponed repairs, a vacant property, or a hard deadline.

What is the East Windsor township sale inspection?

The Bureau of Fire Prevention checks smoke detectors, carbon monoxide detectors and the fire extinguisher before a sale. The township's Selling Your Home page gives the steps: complete the Fire Inspection Form, then deliver or mail it with a $50 check or money order payable to East Windsor Township. Cards are refused, and the township asks for a week to process. A call follows to set the inspection, held mornings on varying days.

The resulting certificate lasts 60 days, so fix a closing date before booking. The inspector reviews how well the detectors work and how old they are, the extinguisher, the record of work and site conditions. Smoke detectors may be no older than 10 years and carbon monoxide detectors no older than 7, going by the manufacturer's label. A 2A10BC extinguisher with this year's tag must be in the kitchen, though it need not be mounted. Failing means repeating the process and paying a $25 re-inspection fee.

The township answers at 609-443-4000, extension 406, from the Municipal Building at 16 Lanning Boulevard.

Does East Windsor require a Certificate of Occupancy at resale?

The township's Certificate of Occupancy page names three residential triggers: new construction, additions, and reconstruction after fire, storm or vehicle damage. A plain resale does not appear among them. The Construction Department also issues continued certificates and certificates of approval, so ask whether anything applies to your property, particularly if a reconstruction job never received a final sign-off.

For a rented house, the construction page sends owners to the East Windsor Health Department at extension 416 for lead-based paint inspections in rental dwellings.

Where is East Windsor and what surrounds it?

In Mercer County, East Windsor covers 15.57 square miles where the Delaware Valley meets the Raritan Valley, an outer-ring New York suburb that also touches the Philadelphia metro area. Its neighbors are Robbinsville and West Windsor in Mercer, Cranbury, Monroe and Plainsboro in Middlesex, and Millstone and Upper Freehold in Monmouth. The independent borough of Hightstown sits wholly inside East Windsor, making the pair one of 21 doughnut towns in New Jersey.

Windsor Township divided on February 9, 1797, producing East and West Windsor, and East Windsor was incorporated on February 21, 1798. Growth arrived late: 2,298 residents in 1960, then 11,736 in 1970 and 21,041 in 1980. Twin Rivers, home to 7,878 people in 2020, was described in a state guide as New Jersey's first planned unit development. If your home is in Twin Rivers, ask the community association what paperwork it expects at resale.

How good is East Windsor's access to highways and transit?

Several major highways meet here. Turnpike Exit 8 is inside the township and feeds Route 33 and Route 133, the Hightstown Bypass. U.S. Route 130 crosses the western part, with county routes 535 and 539 adding local links. Of roughly 93 miles of road, 69 belong to the municipality.

Suburban Transit's 300 line goes to Port Authority in Midtown and its 600 line to Wall Street. The nearest NJ Transit rail stop is Princeton Junction, with a rush-hour shuttle, and Mercer County runs a shuttle along Route 130. Hospitals within reach include Penn Medicine Princeton Medical Center, about 7 miles away in Plainsboro, Robert Wood Johnson University Hospital's Hamilton division, about 10 miles, and CentraState in Freehold, about 17 miles. The average commute is 26.8 minutes.

What jobs and schools are tied to East Windsor?

The township has a pharmaceutical cluster. Hovione, CoreTech, Aprecia, Sabinsa, Novotec, Aurobindo and Windsor Labs all have sites there, and Route 130 carries much of the retail. Freehold Raceway Mall, Quaker Bridge Mall and Princeton Market Fair are short drives.

The East Windsor Regional School District serves East Windsor and Hightstown with six schools and 5,138 students in 2022-23. Walter C. Black and Ethel McKnight cover kindergarten through grade 2, Perry L. Drew and Grace N. Rogers cover grades 3 to 5, Melvin H. Kreps Middle School takes grades 6 to 8, and Hightstown High School takes grades 9 to 12. Eighth graders anywhere in Mercer County can apply to Mercer County Technical Schools, which charge no tuition.

What do the Census numbers say about East Windsor housing?

For 2020 through 2024, the middle owned home is valued at $397,400 and median household income is $105,208. About 45 percent of adults 25 and older hold at least a bachelor's degree, and roughly 44 percent of residents use another language at home.

What will an East Windsor seller pay, and where does the deed go?

The state realty transfer fee is the seller's. Using $397,400, the Census middle value for owned homes in East Windsor, the state schedule gives about $3,190. Mercer County's Clerk page adds that the graduated charge on sales of $1 million and up, starting at 1 percent, moved to the seller as of July 10, 2025.

  • Township check: $50 with the Fire Inspection Form, plus $25 if a second visit is needed.
  • Filing the deed: the Mercer County Clerk charges $43 for a regular deed's first page and $10 for every added page.
  • How to pay: transfer fees go in by cash, cashier's check, money order, attorney trust account or business escrow account, with certified or bank checks required above $10,000.
  • State form: a GIT/REP seller certification accompanies the deed.

The Records Room welcomes the public on weekdays between 8:30 and 4:30, and the Indexing Section's number is 609-989-6476.

Is a fire inspection required to sell in East Windsor?

Yes for a single-family home or condominium. The Bureau of Fire Prevention certifies detectors and an extinguisher before the sale, at $50, with a certificate good for 60 days.

What detector ages does East Windsor accept?

Smoke detectors up to 10 years old and carbon monoxide detectors up to 7, per the manufacturer's label. The kitchen also needs a 2A10BC extinguisher with a current-year tag.

What if the East Windsor inspector fails my house?

Fix the items and run the process again with a $25 re-inspection fee. The certificate expires after 60 days, so book early enough to leave room for a second visit.

Will a resale in East Windsor require a Certificate of Occupancy?

The township's residential list covers new construction, additions and reconstruction. If your house was rebuilt after a fire or storm, ask Code Enforcement whether a final certificate was issued.

Who files an East Windsor deed?

The Mercer County Clerk. A regular deed runs $43 for page one and $10 for each page after, and the transfer fee has to arrive by an accepted method such as cash, cashier's check, money order or attorney trust account.

Ewing at a glance

Selling in Ewing?

What makes selling a house in Ewing Township different?

Ewing requires every home sold in the township to pass a housing inspection first, so the main variable in a fast sale is how quickly the property can pass that check. The rest of the process is the usual New Jersey deed, transfer fee and tax filings.

Ewing sits in Mercer County on the Delaware River, directly north and west of Trenton. It covers about 15.6 square miles, and the 2020 Census counted 37,264 residents, the highest count in the township's history. The Census Bureau estimated 39,030 people in July 2025, a rise of 4.5 percent from the 2020 base. The 2020 density was about 2,450 people per square mile of land.

How did Ewing Township grow into the community it is today?

Ewing became a township on February 22, 1834, cut from Trenton Township and named in honor of Charles Ewing, a former chief justice of the New Jersey Supreme Court. It joined the new Mercer County in 1838. Before that the land was mostly farms and small hamlets: Carleton is now Ewing, Cross Keys is Ewingville, and Birmingham is West Trenton.

The township grew as a suburb of Trenton through the 20th century. Its population rose from 6,942 in 1930 to 26,628 by 1960 and has stayed between about 32,800 and 37,300 since 1970. Blocks near the Trenton line are distinctly urban, while most of the township is residential subdivisions.

Neighborhood names show up in listings and appraisals, so use the local one. Examples include Ewingville, West Trenton, Prospect Heights, Fernwood, Hillwood Lakes, Parkway Village, Scudders Falls and Wilburtha. Many were built in separate phases, and house styles change noticeably from one to the next.

What do Census figures say about Ewing homes and renters?

Ewing prices sit below the national median value, and rental households make up a third of the township. The table lists the 2020 to 2024 Census QuickFacts estimates against national figures.

Which employers and institutions anchor the Ewing market?

Ewing hosts several large public employers, which keeps demand for housing steady among staff who want a short commute. The Katzenbach School for the Deaf and the Trenton-Mercer Airport are also located in the township.

Church and Dwight moved its corporate headquarters from Princeton to Ewing in 2013. The township also absorbed a major loss: the Naval Air Warfare Center Trenton on Parkway Avenue operated from 1953 until 1997 and closed under the 1993 base closure recommendations, ending nearly 700 civilian positions. The Jones Farm, the last working farm in Ewing, shut at the end of 2022.

  • Education and public safety: The College of New Jersey and State Police headquarters.
  • State agencies: the Department of Transportation headquarters and Trenton Psychiatric Hospital.
  • Private employers: Church and Dwight, plus the Community Blood Council of New Jersey.

Which roads and rail lines serve Ewing homes?

Four major roads cross the township, and the West Trenton rail terminal anchors the commuter side. Interstate 295 crosses the northwest corner, Route 29 follows the Delaware River as the Delaware River Scenic Byway, U.S. Route 206 skirts the southeast, and Route 31 (Pennington Road) runs north to Pennington and Flemington.

West Trenton station is the terminus of SEPTA's West Trenton Line, which mainly carries riders to Philadelphia. NJ Transit buses 601, 607, 608, 609 and 624 connect the township with Trenton. Trenton-Mercer Airport, open since 1929 and served by Frontier Airlines, is also inside Ewing's borders.

The Delaware and Raritan Canal passes near the river, and the strip of land along it is part of the Delaware and Raritan Canal State Park. Homes along River Road and Route 29 sit near the water, so check flood-zone status with the township before quoting a price to a buyer who asks.

How do schools and weather affect an Ewing house?

Ewing Public Schools run prekindergarten through twelfth grade in one district, with five schools: Antheil, Lore and Parkway elementary schools, Fisher Middle School and Ewing High School. Enrollment was 3,444 students in the 2020 to 2021 school year. The district is also known for the 1946 case Everson v. Board of Education, a U.S. Supreme Court decision on bus transport for parochial school students.

The climate is hot-summer humid continental. Based on 1991 to 2020 normals, the township averages 48.2 inches of precipitation a year and about 8 inches of snow in each of January and February.

That much rain is why the housing inspector looks at grading and drainage, roofs, gutters and foundation walls. Fixing a downspout that empties against the foundation costs little and removes an easy objection before the inspection.

What does Ewing's resale inspection check?

Every dwelling or commercial building offered for resale must be inspected and approved by the Ewing Division of Housing, and the residential fee on the township's 2025 form is $125. The inspector works from the International Property Maintenance Code and township ordinances. Requests can be made through the township's SDL portal, which needs an account, or through the Construction Office at 1666 Pennington Road, 609-883-2900, extension 7676.

The township's printed checklist is not limited to these items, but they come up often:

  • Smoke alarms on every level, using ten-year sealed lithium battery single-station units, and carbon monoxide alarms within 10 feet of sleeping areas.
  • A portable fire extinguisher rated at least 2A-10B:C within 10 feet of the kitchen, mounted no higher than 5 feet, and tagged or receipted within the last 12 months.
  • Ground-fault outlets in kitchens, baths and outdoors, and at least two receptacles per bedroom.
  • Sound handrails, stairs, roofs, windows with screens, and working heating equipment.
  • No double-keyed deadbolts, which the form calls illegal.
  • All open permits closed out, and a well water certificate where a well serves the house.

Some repairs may need Uniform Construction Code permits, so call the office before hiring a contractor.

What if the Ewing house is a rental?

Rental houses carry extra paperwork in Ewing, and the registration status should be settled before a sale. Under township ordinance 10-07, residential rentals must be registered every year regardless of tenant changes, with the registration and rental fire prevention forms due January 31. Landlords also need a property maintenance inspection whenever a tenant changes.

If you sell a rental, give the buyer the registration record, the latest fire prevention form and any open violation notices. A buyer who wants to occupy the house will need the unit vacated on a schedule written into the contract.

What are the closing costs and recording steps in Ewing?

The seller pays the state Realty Transfer Fee, and the deed is recorded with the Mercer County Clerk in Trenton, whose office has kept property records since 1838. For total consideration of $350,000 or less, the state schedule runs $2.00 per $500 up to $150,000, $3.35 per $500 from $150,000 to $200,000 and $3.90 per $500 from $200,000 to $350,000. Ask the closing attorney for the final figure.

The county charges $43 for the first page of a regular deed and $10 for each additional page. Realty transfer fees must be paid by cash, cashier's check, money order, attorney trust account or business escrow account, and amounts over $10,000 by certified or bank check. Mercer's land records page also notes that the transfer fee on sales of $1 million and above, often called the mansion tax, changed on July 10, 2025 so that the seller pays it.

New Jersey residents sign a GIT/REP-3 at closing. A nonresident owner owes an estimated payment of at least 2 percent of the price unless an exemption applies.

More questions about Ewing, NJ

Is an inspection required to sell a house in Ewing?

Yes. The Division of Housing must inspect and approve every dwelling offered for resale in the township. The residential fee on the 2025 form is $125, and requests go through the SDL portal or the Construction Office at 609-883-2900, extension 7676.

What alarms does a Ewing resale inspection require?

The township asks for smoke alarms on every level, using ten-year sealed lithium battery single-station units, and carbon monoxide alarms within 10 feet of sleeping areas. It also asks for a labeled fire extinguisher near the kitchen that is tagged or receipted within 12 months.

How much does the Mercer County Clerk charge to record a deed?

A regular deed costs $43 for the first page and $10 for each added page. The state transfer fee is paid separately at recording and is set by the sale price. The county clerk accepts cash, cashier's check, money order, attorney trust account or business escrow account for that fee.

Do I have to register a rental before selling it in Ewing?

Registration is a yearly requirement under ordinance 10-07, with forms due January 31, so it should already be on file. Landlords also need a property maintenance inspection on each tenant change. Bring the paperwork to the sale so the buyer sees a clean record.

Can I sell a Ewing house with open permits?

Open permits must be closed out before the resale inspection can be passed, according to the township's inspection list. Call the Construction Office to learn what final inspections are outstanding. Some repairs also need new Uniform Construction Code permits before work begins.
