What moves a Hamilton Township, Mercer County, sale along fastest?

Timing comes down to a Certificate of Approval from the township's housing inspectors, a settled tax balance and a deed recorded in Trenton. This page covers the Hamilton beside Trenton, which is a separate place from the Atlantic County township with the same name.

It is the most populous municipality in Mercer County, with a Census Bureau estimate of 94,157 residents for July 1, 2025. Owners live in 71.6 percent of homes, and the typical owner-occupied value is $335,500. A cash buyer who accepts the house as it stands removes the loan approval and repair requests that often stretch a conventional timeline.

How is Hamilton Township laid out for a seller?

Hamilton covers 39.44 square miles and is the largest suburb of Trenton, the state capital, which lies to its west. It has no true downtown. Separate communities act as commercial centers instead: Mercerville (13,447 residents in 2020), Hamilton Square (12,679), White Horse (9,791), Yardville (6,965) and Groveville (3,106).

Incorporation came on April 11, 1842, and the name comes from Hamilton Square. Open space is a draw: Veterans Park fills 350 acres inside the township, Mercer County Park's 2,500 acres adjoin it to the north, and Grounds For Sculpture occupies 42 acres. Retirement communities and assisted-living facilities have gone up near Robert Wood Johnson University Hospital Hamilton, and new restaurants, banks and stores have opened along Route 33.

  • Mercerville and Hamilton Square: the two most populous census-designated places.
  • White Horse: in the southern part of the township, where the 1733 Isaac Pearson House stands.
  • Groveville: the smallest of the five census-designated places.

The Isaac Watson House of 1708, the oldest house in Mercer County, stands near White Horse. The Postal Service officially treats many Hamilton addresses as Trenton, so state the township name in your advertising.

Which Hamilton Township figures should guide my asking price?

What approval does Hamilton Township require before occupancy changes?

Before any change in occupancy of a house or apartment, the Office of Housing Inspection and Landlord Compliance has to issue a Certificate of Approval stating that the building and premises meet township ordinances. The township names life safety as the first priority of the inspection.

Applications go through the Change of Occupancy Application Portal or on paper to the office. A Change of Occupancy Checklist is published, and reading it before the inspector arrives is the cheapest way to avoid a second visit. The township does not inspect houses for lead on request, so a seller who wants a lead test must hire a private inspector.

  • Apply once you have a signed contract so the approval is fresh at closing.
  • Check smoke and carbon monoxide alarms, since state rules require a certificate valid for six months on one-family and two-family sales.
  • Fix visible safety problems, such as loose rails and missing detectors, before the appointment.

The construction office keeps a house's blueprints for 10 years, so ask for plans if you need to show a buyer what was built. The Land Use Office can confirm a parcel's zoning designation.

How do assessments and appeals work in Hamilton Township?

The Mercer County Board of Taxation, at 640 South Broad Street in Trenton, certifies assessments and hears appeals. Regular appeals are due April 1, appeals over added or omitted assessments are due December 1, and in-person filing runs from 8:30 a.m. until 4:00 p.m. Postcards with the new assessment go out at the end of January, so read yours before deciding to file.

The county's Property Information Portal shows property record cards, sales, deeds and tax information, which helps you locate comparable sales near your street before you decide whether to file. Request a written tax payoff from the township collector before closing.

What will a Hamilton Township seller pay, and where does the deed go?

The state's Realty Transfer Fee falls on the seller at recording. For a price above $350,000 the rate starts at $2.90 per $500 on the first $150,000, and the schedule steps up in higher brackets, so a $450,000 sale lands near $3,695. The county clerk adds that deeds above $1,000,000 recorded since July 10, 2025 carry a revised fee under a new state law.

Real estate transfers are recorded at the Mercer County Clerk's Office, 209 South Broad Street in Trenton, where title searchers and the public can view a property's history in the records room or online. Resident sellers sign the GIT/REP-3 residency certification. Sellers who live elsewhere prepay Gross Income Tax of 2 percent of the price or more.

  • State transfer fee, set by the rate table.
  • Mortgage and lien payoffs.
  • The seller's share of the quarter's property tax.
  • Certificate and inspection fees set by the township.

What if I am selling a Hamilton Township rental?

About 28 percent of occupied homes in Hamilton are rented, and typical rent is $1,634. The same housing inspection office that approves owner sales handles any change of occupancy in a house, dwelling unit or apartment, so a rental turning over to a new tenant or a new owner passes through it as well.

Gather leases, move-out dates and repair records before you apply. A buyer who plans to rent the house will need approval for the next tenancy as well, so a clean inspection record helps the sale.

How do highways, trains and schools shape Hamilton Township demand?

Hamilton is the only New Jersey municipality hosting Interstate 95 along with both of its auxiliary routes, I-195 and I-295, plus U.S. Routes 130 and 206 and Routes 29, 33 and 156. The township lies about 65 miles from New York City and 35 miles from Philadelphia. The Hamilton station on Sloan Avenue, off I-295 Exit 65B, serves NJ Transit's Northeast Corridor and logged 3,635 average weekday boardings in 2025, the eighth-highest in the state.

The Hamilton Township School District runs 23 schools, including three high schools named Nottingham (North), Hamilton West and Steinert (East), and reported 11,816 students in the 2021 to 2022 school year. Water comes from Aqua New Jersey or Trenton Water Works, so confirm which utility serves the house.

More questions about Hamilton (Mercer), NJ

Which approval must a seller get in Hamilton Township, Mercer County?

A Certificate of Approval from the Office of Housing Inspection and Landlord Compliance, required before a change of occupancy. Apply through the township portal or with the office's paper forms.

Where is an assessment appeal filed in Hamilton Township?

With the Mercer County Board of Taxation at 640 South Broad Street in Trenton by April 1. Appeals over added or omitted assessments are due December 1.

Will the township test my house for lead before a sale?

No, it does not test houses for lead on request. A seller who wants a test has to hire a private inspector.

Which office records a Hamilton Township deed?

The Mercer County Clerk's Office at 209 South Broad Street in Trenton. Deeds above $1,000,000 recorded since July 10, 2025 carry a revised fee under the new state law.

Why do some Hamilton addresses say Trenton?

The Postal Service officially treats many Hamilton addresses as Trenton even though the house is in Hamilton Township. Name the township in your listing so buyers can find the right tax and school information.

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

East Brunswick at a glance

Selling in East Brunswick?
We buy East Brunswick houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.
Get My Cash Offer →

How fast can an East Brunswick house actually sell?

An East Brunswick owner can put the house on the market, deal directly with a cash buyer, or sell privately to someone they know. Timing decides it. Marketing a house in a township this size can draw strong interest, yet it still involves staging, showings, an inspection and a lender's appraisal. A direct sale gives up some price in return for a closing date you set.

The Census Bureau estimated East Brunswick's population at 50,678 on July 1, 2025, up from 49,715 in 2020. Owners occupy eight in ten homes. Reasons people hurry include an inheritance, a rental they are done managing, or a house that needs more updating than they want to fund.

  • Agent listing: works for a house in good shape when the calendar is loose.
  • Direct cash sale: works when repairs are pending, tenants are in place, or the closing date is fixed.
  • Private sale: possible if you handle the paperwork yourself, and the township's detector certificate still applies.

How did East Brunswick become a commuter township?

East Brunswick was incorporated on February 28, 1860, carved from parts of Monroe and North Brunswick. It stayed mostly farmland until suburban building began in the 1930s, and the New Jersey Turnpike extension of 1952 set off the big surge: the population went from 5,699 in 1950 to 19,965 in 1960. The Old Bridge section in the southeast was listed as a historic district in 1977.

Geography still shapes lots and prices. East Brunswick holds 21.78 square miles of land along the Raritan River's southern shore. Lawrence Brook and Farrington Lake run along the western edge, the South River marks the east, and Manalapan Brook drains much of the south. It touches Edison, Helmetta, Milltown, Monroe, New Brunswick, North Brunswick, Old Bridge, Sayreville, South River, South Brunswick and Spotswood. Since the 2000 census, New Jersey's population center has fallen inside East Brunswick.

How do Route 18, the Turnpike and buses affect an East Brunswick sale?

Commuting drives much of the demand. The township sits at Exit 9 of the Turnpike, and Route 18 crosses its eastern half toward New Brunswick, U.S. Route 1 and the Shore. County routes 527 and 535 pass through as well, with the Garden State Parkway and Interstate 287 a short drive away in neighboring towns. Midtown Manhattan and Center City Philadelphia each take 45 to 60 minutes by car depending on traffic, and Newark Liberty International Airport is about 24 miles off.

NJ Transit's 138 goes to Port Authority in Manhattan and the 68 to Jersey City, while routes 811, 815 and 818 stay local. Suburban Transit coaches to New York depart the Transportation Center and Tower Center every 10 to 15 minutes and take 30 to 50. Road mileage totals about 206, roughly 176 of it municipal.

Census data put the typical commute at 36.5 minutes, against 30.5 statewide.

What business and shopping draws support East Brunswick values?

Brunswick Square Mall, at Route 18 and Rues Lane, opened in 1970 and offers about 769,000 square feet of leasable space. Near the Turnpike and Route 18 stand the two 23-story Tower Center office towers and a 12-story Hilton, and Wipro opened its U.S. headquarters there in March 2023. At the quieter end, Giamarese Farm and Orchards has run on 35 acres of Fresh Ponds Road since 1941.

Which schools serve East Brunswick homes?

East Brunswick Public Schools operates 11 schools from pre-K to grade 12, with 8,163 students in 2024-25. Eight elementary schools cover the early grades: Bowne-Munro, Central, Chittick, Frost, Irwin, Lawrence Brook, Memorial and Warnsdorfer. Hammarskjold Upper Elementary takes grades 5 and 6, Churchill Junior High takes grades 7 to 9, and East Brunswick High School takes grades 10 to 12. Middlesex County eighth graders may also apply to the free-tuition Middlesex County Magnet Schools, one campus of which is in East Brunswick.

Confirm with the district which elementary school your street feeds before you list.

How expensive is East Brunswick compared with the rest of New Jersey?

The 2020 through 2024 survey estimates value the middle owned home at $521,900, about $67,500 over the statewide $454,400, with owners living in 80.0 percent of homes. Roughly 58 percent of adults have at least a bachelor's degree, and a third of residents were born abroad.

Does East Brunswick want a Certificate of Occupancy before closing?

No. The township's construction page says East Brunswick neither requires nor issues a Certificate of Occupancy for residential resale or rentals. A home receives its certificate when built, and later only new improvements get inspected. Questions go to Construction Inspection at 732-390-6875.

Fire safety follows its own track. Carbon monoxide alarms near bedrooms have been mandatory in one and two family homes since April 7, 2003. In 2025 the council also adopted Ordinance 25-30, which calls for smoke and carbon monoxide detector inspections and certificates when residential units are sold, leased or newly occupied. In the introduced text the fee was $50 per unit with more than 10 business days of notice before the change of occupant, $75 at 4 to 10 days, and $125 under 4, plus $20 for a re-inspection after a failure. Ask the township for today's schedule and book early, since the late fee is the highest.

What will an East Brunswick seller pay at closing?

State law puts the realty transfer fee on the seller. Running the state's tiers against $521,900, the Census figure for a middle-priced owned home here, gives roughly $4,385, and a price above $1,000,000 adds a graduated percentage charge.

  • Transfer fee: collected from the seller at filing, using a tiered rate per $500 of price.
  • Detector certificate: a township charge that climbs as the closing date nears.
  • Payoffs: your mortgage and any liens come out of the proceeds.
  • Tax form: a GIT/REP certification travels with the deed and decides whether a nonresident seller must prepay.

Which office files the deed on an East Brunswick sale?

The Middlesex County Clerk handles it, at the County Administration Building, 75 Bayard Street, fourth floor, in New Brunswick. Weekday hours end at 4:10, but the office asks that you arrive by 4. The registry's number is 732-745-3002. Its posted schedule lists $45 for a deed's first page and $10 for each page after that, with a $6 name fee in some cases. A free Property Alert service emails you when a filed document matches your property.

What if my East Brunswick house has been a short-term rental?

Chapter 182 of the township code governs short-term rentals, and the council amended it through Ordinance 25-34 in 2025. If you hosted guests, read the current chapter or call the township before describing the house's rental history to a buyer.

More questions about East Brunswick, NJ

Is a resale inspection mandatory in East Brunswick?

No Certificate of Occupancy is needed for a residential resale. A 2025 ordinance does call for smoke and carbon monoxide detector certification on sale, so ask the township how to book it.

What sets the timeline for a cash closing in East Brunswick?

The contract does. With no lender appraisal involved, the pace depends mainly on the title search, the detector certificate, and the deed filing with the Middlesex County Clerk.

Is the transfer fee on an East Brunswick sale mine or the buyer's?

It is the seller's. A $521,900 price, the Census figure for the middle owned home, produces about $4,385 under the state schedule.

Where is the deed filed after closing here?

With the Middlesex County Clerk, 75 Bayard Street, fourth floor, New Brunswick, through the registry at 732-745-3002.

Can a house with tenants still be sold in East Brunswick?

Yes. The ordinance reaches sales, leases and other occupancy, so time the detector inspection around the tenants' move-out or the closing.

What should I know before selling a house in Edison, NJ?

Edison is a Middlesex County township of about 30 square miles where the sale usually hinges on one local document, the Residential Resale Certificate, plus a state smoke certificate that has to come first. Nothing about those steps is hard, but each has lead time, so start them as soon as a buyer signs a contract.

The Census Bureau counts 109,077 residents for 2025 and 38,098 households. Roughly 61 percent of homes are owner occupied, and owners report a median home value of $496,900 for 2020 to 2024. Median household income is $125,145, and 47.7 percent of residents were born abroad.

How did Edison get its name, and why does it matter to a seller?

The township carries the inventor's name because voters changed it in 1954, and it sits on the ground where Thomas Edison ran his Menlo Park laboratory from 1876. The place was earlier called Raritan Township and was carved out of Piscataway and Woodbridge. Colonial-era buildings still stand near Piscatawaytown in South Edison, and three are listed nationally: the Laing House, the Benjamin Shotwell House and the Homestead Farm at Oak Ridge.

The township has many named sections, among them Stelton, Menlo Park, Oak Tree, Raritan Manor, Clara Barton, Lindenau and Washington Park. A house that has changed hands more than once is more likely to carry a finished basement, deck or addition from an earlier owner, and those are the items the township inspector checks for permits.

What does the Edison resale certificate require?

Edison Township Ordinance 14-1.6 says a Certificate for Change of Ownership must be obtained before the property closes, and the township form warns of fines up to $2,000 for skipping it. The application fee is $150, paid by certified check, credit card or money order. The form says no cash, no personal checks and no refunds. Code Enforcement takes the application by email at the resale address printed on the form and then calls for a card payment.

Timing is the part that trips people up. One line of the form asks for the inspection at least four weeks before the closing date, and another says three weeks, so plan on four. A smoke certificate must already exist before the resale certificate can be issued, and the inspector wants a copy on site.

What the Edison inspector checks on a one or two family home
AreaWhat the form asks for
PermitsAdditions, finished basements or attics, garage conversions, patios, decks, pools and spas need verified permits
Pools and spasFence and childproof gate
Stairs and railsSecure guardrails and handrails; stair riser openings under 4 inches
MechanicalsWater heater with relief valve and piping ending 6 inches off the floor; tight flue connections; shut-off valves on gas appliances
DryerVented outside, not into a garage, attic or basement
OutsideHouse numbers at least 4 inches high at the front
InteriorWorking GFI outlets, no keyed locks on bedroom doors or inside egress doors, no junk or debris

Source: Edison Township Residential Resale Certificate Application.

What if work was done on the house without a permit?

  • The form says the current owner must resolve it, even if a previous owner did the work.
  • You pull a compliance permit, have the work inspected and close the permit before the certificate is issued.
  • Before the inspection, check the Building Department for open permits and ask the Tax Assessor whether improvements such as a finished basement are on the township record.
  • The ordinance covers every change of ownership, so a sale to a cash buyer still needs the certificate before closing.

Open permits are the most common reason an Edison closing slips. Ask the Building Department for a permit history on the address as soon as you list.

What does Edison look like to a buyer?

Edison surrounds the borough of Metuchen and touches East Brunswick, Highland Park, New Brunswick, Piscataway, Sayreville, South Plainfield and Woodbridge in Middlesex County, plus Clark, Plainfield and Scotch Plains in Union County. The township sits roughly 27 miles from both Midtown Manhattan and Trenton.

  • Rail: Edison station in South Edison runs NJ Transit Northeast Corridor trains to Newark Penn, New York Penn and Trenton, and North Edison residents may be closer to Metropark or Metuchen stations.
  • Roads: Route 27, Route 440, U.S. Route 1, Interstate 287 and about five miles of the New Jersey Turnpike, with Exit 10 inside the township.
  • Jobs: Raritan Center, a 2,300 acre business park, plus the state's largest private convention center, warehouse hubs and an Amazon fulfillment center.

Census workers here spend 33.9 minutes getting to their jobs on average.

How does Edison's weather show up in a home inspection?

The township's climate is humid subtropical, and rain and melted snow add up to about 49.6 inches a year, the wettest stretch running through late summer, and snow falls several times each winter. Recorded extremes run from minus 17 degrees in 1934 to 106 degrees in 1936 and 1949.

A buyer's inspector will therefore look closely at the roof, gutters and basement walls, and the township checklist adds the water heater and stair rails. Fixing a damp basement corner or a loose guardrail before you list costs less than negotiating it after the inspection report.

Which schools serve Edison homes?

Edison Township Public Schools serve pre-kindergarten through grade 12 and split the township between two high schools. Homes in the south feed Edison High School, and homes in the north feed J.P. Stevens High School. The district reported 16,268 students across 19 schools for 2021-22. Families also look at the Greater Brunswick Charter School and the Middlesex County Magnet Schools, which accept applications from eighth graders countywide.

When you list, name the attendance zone for the street you are on. The zone is part of how a listing is described.

How do property tax appeals and closing costs work for an Edison seller?

Property tax appeals go to the Middlesex County Board of Taxation, which has said it will not hold virtual hearings. The state deadline is April 1, moved to May 1 where a municipality has done a revaluation.

At closing the seller pays the state realty transfer fee. The state's own example shows $1,910 on a $325,000 deed with no exemption. Edison sellers who live in New Jersey sign GIT/REP-3 to record the deed, while nonresident sellers use GIT/REP-1 or GIT/REP-2 unless they qualify under a seller's assurance.

Where does the deed get recorded in Edison?

The Middlesex County Clerk records every deed for Edison at the County Administration Building, 75 Bayard Street, New Brunswick. The office takes walk-ins on weekdays, opening at 8:30 and closing at 4:10, with a 4:00 arrival cutoff. Paper filings need a cover sheet, and skipping it adds a $20 indexing charge. The deed must say "Prepared by," list tax block, lot and consideration, and carry a return address.

Most Edison closings go through an attorney or title company that records electronically, so this matters mainly when you sell without one.

More questions about Edison, NJ

How much does the Edison resale certificate cost?

The township form lists a $150 fee. It must be paid by certified check, credit card or money order, and the form states there are no cash payments, no personal checks and no refunds. Fines of up to $2,000 apply if you close without the certificate.

Do I need the smoke certificate before the Edison inspection?

Yes. The form says the smoke certificate is required before the resale certificate can be issued. If the Fire Prevention inspection happens first, give the inspector a copy at the resale visit or email it to the township's resale address.

Can I sell an Edison house with a finished basement that has no permit?

You can sell it, but the certificate will not issue until a permit is obtained, the work passes inspection and the permit is closed. Check with the Building Department and the Tax Assessor before you schedule the inspection.

Which county office records an Edison deed?

The Middlesex County Clerk in New Brunswick. The office is open weekdays from 8:30 a.m. and requires arrival by 4:00 p.m., and paper documents need a cover sheet.

What is the deadline to appeal an Edison property tax assessment?

April 1 of the tax year, or May 1 when the township completed a revaluation. File with the Middlesex County Board of Taxation. Properties assessed above $1,000,000 can go straight to the State Tax Court.

Freehold at a glance

Selling in Freehold?
We buy Freehold houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.

Is selling in Freehold Township, NJ the same as selling in Freehold Borough?

No. Freehold Township and Freehold Borough are separate municipalities with separate offices, and the township completely surrounds the borough. New Jersey counts this as one of 21 pairs of doughnut towns, where one municipality wraps around another, so check which one your deed and tax bill name before you call anyone.

The township covers 38.65 square miles of land in western Monmouth County. The Census Bureau estimates 36,052 residents for July 2025, up 1.9% from the April 2020 base but still below the 36,184 counted in 2010.

Homes here skew toward owners: 83.7% of housing is owner-occupied, and 94.2% of residents lived in the same house a year earlier. Median value of owner-occupied homes is $553,600 for 2020-2024, with median gross rent of $2,194.

How does Freehold Township's history show up in a house sale today?

It shows up in the street names, the farmland and the parks. The township was first formed on October 31, 1693, and the legislature incorporated it on February 21, 1798. The word freehold is an English legal term for fee simple ownership, which is the kind of title you are transferring.

The Battle of Monmouth was fought on June 28, 1778, on ground now preserved as Monmouth Battlefield State Park, partly inside the township. Later, highways such as U.S. Route 9 and Route 33 let residents commute to Newark, Philadelphia and New York, and large neighborhoods of single-family homes followed.

Commercial growth came in layers. Brockway Glass built a plant off Center Street in 1955 and closed it in 1991, 3M opened a tape plant in 1957, CentraState Medical Center opened in 1971 as Freehold Area Hospital, and Freehold Raceway Mall opened in 1990 as the second largest mall in the state. Farms with crops, thoroughbreds, sod and orchards still operate in the township.

What does Freehold Township require before a house can be sold?

Freehold Township requires both a Certificate of Continued Occupancy (CCO) inspection and a fire inspection whenever a residential property is sold or rented. The two applications must go to the Housing Department together, each with its own check or money order, and the township does not take cash or cards.

The inspection appointment can be scheduled only after both applications and payments are in. A CCO issued for a resale is valid for up to 120 calendar days, or until occupancy changes, so do not apply so early that it lapses before closing. For scheduling, call the Department of Zoning and Housing Enforcement at 732-294-2066.

Freehold Township CCO and fire inspection rules for resales
ItemTownship rule
ApplicationsCCO and fire application filed together, one payment each
PaymentCheck or money order only
Validity of a resale CCOUp to 120 calendar days
Validity of a rental CCOUp to 60 calendar days
Open permitsAll permits must be closed before the CCO is issued
Well or septicHealth Department approval, 732-294-2060

What does the Freehold Township inspector look for?

The township's own checklist is mainly about safety and open permits, and it states that buyers should still hire a private inspector. Any violation the inspector considers a safety issue must be fixed even if it is not on the list.

  • Permits: work done without permits, such as water heaters, furnaces, AC, decks, sheds, fences and finished basements, must be permitted and closed first.
  • Utilities must be on, and the house number must be six inches high and visible from the street.
  • Doors: entry doors with deadbolts need an inside thumb latch, and double-key deadbolts and slide bolts are not allowed.
  • Electrical: GFCI outlets within six feet of every sink, and covers on all outlets, switches and junction boxes.
  • Garage: entry doors need a solid core wood or steel door with a 20-minute fire rating.
  • Dryer vents must be flexible metal, and a sump pump needs its own outlet and must discharge outdoors.
  • Pools need self-closing, self-latching gates and must be running or closed.

Smoke and carbon monoxide alarms are handled on the separate fire checklist. Alarms are required on every level including the basement and within ten feet of bedrooms, and detectors must be replaced every ten years.

What if the Freehold Township house cannot pass the CCO before closing?

The township offers a document called Transfer of Title, No Occupancy, which lets a closing go forward while the buyer fixes the remaining items. The state still requires every property to pass the fire inspection before the sale, so the smoke and carbon monoxide work cannot be skipped.

The process runs in steps. Both applications and payments go in first, and the inspector lists deficiencies, sometimes marking the house as having too many items to list. The buyer's attorney then writes a letter on the township's sample, agreeing there will be no occupancy until a new inspection and CCO, and agreeing to hold the township harmless. After the fire inspection passes and the letter is filed, the Housing Department emails the document for closing.

After closing the buyer owns the repair list and schedules the final CCO inspection. This path suits a cash buyer who plans to renovate. Rental properties follow stricter rules: they must be registered, vacant at inspection, freshly painted and, if built before 1978, supported by a lead-safe certificate that lasts two years.

How do estates, trusts and co-owners handle state forms at a Freehold Township closing?

Each seller on the deed completes a GIT/REP residency form, and the Monmouth County Clerk will not record the deed without one. Married couples who file a joint New Jersey return can sign one form, but unmarried co-owners each sign their own.

  • Estates: the estate completes the form under its own residency status, signed by the executors or the administrator if there was no will. One form can carry several executors' signatures.
  • Trusts: the trustee signs for the trust, and a trustee who is also a beneficiary signs a second form in a personal capacity.
  • Percent of ownership: if one owner holds 50% and two others hold 25% each, each form shows that share.
  • LLCs and corporations complete the GIT/REP-3 and check the box for sellers that are not individuals.

For a nonresident seller, the state's formula multiplies gain by 10.75% but never lets the estimated payment fall below 2% of the deed consideration. Sheriff's sales and bankruptcy trust sales are the only exceptions to the form requirement.

What do roads, schools and employers mean for Freehold Township buyers?

Buyers weigh the commute first. Mean travel time to work is 30.9 minutes (2020-2024). Route 9, Route 33, Route 18 and Route 79 cross the township, with county routes 522, 524, 527 and 537, and Interstate 195 is reachable through Howell on Route 9 or Jackson on County Route 537. Garden State Parkway Exit 100 is about ten miles east.

NJ Transit buses 131, 135 and 139 run along Route 9 to the Port Authority Bus Terminal. The nearest rail stops are Aberdeen-Matawan, Asbury Park and Long Branch, and the SeaStreak ferry from Highlands is a 25 to 30 minute drive from the east side of the township.

High school students attend Freehold Township High School or Freehold High School, both in the Freehold Regional High School District, and assignment depends on the home address. CentraState Medical Center, a 287-bed hospital inside the township, ranks as the county's fourth-largest employer. The township sits on the northern edge of the humid subtropical climate zone, next to the humid continental zone.

More questions about Freehold, NJ

Does Freehold Township require an inspection when I sell?

Yes. Freehold Township requires a Certificate of Continued Occupancy inspection and a fire inspection for every residential sale or rental. Both applications are submitted together to the Housing Department, each with a check or money order.

How long is a Freehold Township resale CCO good for?

Up to 120 calendar days from the date of issue, or until the occupancy changes, whichever comes first. A rental CCO lasts only up to 60 days.

Can a Freehold Township house close without passing the CCO?

Yes, with a Transfer of Title, No Occupancy document. The buyer's attorney signs a letter agreeing there is no occupancy until the final CCO is issued, and the property must still pass the fire inspection first.

Which phone number do I call to schedule a Freehold Township CCO?

Call the Department of Zoning and Housing Enforcement at 732-294-2066. The township's FAQ also lists 732-294-5109, and the zoning office line is 732-294-2068.

Do estates in Freehold Township need special state tax forms?

They need the same GIT/REP form as any seller, filled out in the estate's name. If there was a will, the executors or beneficiaries who sign the deed sign the form; with no will, the administrator signs it.

How can you sell a house fast in Howell, New Jersey?

Howell sellers can hire an agent, go it alone or take a cash purchase. All three meet the township's fire inspection, the one local step nobody skips. Howell is a large, mostly single-family township in Monmouth County, so many sellers have a detached house on a sizeable lot, sometimes with older systems.

  • Agent listing: exposure to the most buyers, which suits a house that shows well, though appraisals, mortgage approval and repair requests stretch the calendar.
  • Private sale: you skip the commission and handle the price, the contract and the alarm inspection yourself.
  • Cash buyer: no lender and no repair haggling, which fits an inherited home, a vacant house or a short move deadline.

Under any of them, book the Fire Bureau inspection early. Failing it for a missing detector is the most avoidable delay in a Howell sale.

Where is Howell Township and how did it grow?

At roughly 61.21 square miles, Howell is Monmouth County's biggest municipality by area, and 60.27 of those miles are land. It borders Colts Neck, Freehold Township and Wall in Monmouth County and Brick, Jackson and Lakewood in Ocean County. Named communities inside the township include Ramtown, Adelphia, Ardena, Land of Pines, Southard and Squankum.

The Legislature carved Howell out of Shrewsbury Township on February 23, 1801. Brick split off in 1850 and Wall in 1851, and Farmingdale became its own borough in 1903. Because the township still surrounds Farmingdale completely, it is one of the state's 21 pairs of doughnut towns.

The area was once iron country. Bog iron fed the Howell Works in the 19th century, and the preserved Allaire Village now sits inside Allaire State Park along the Howell and Wall border. The ground is sandy Outer Coastal Plain soil with pine and oak woods, wetlands and the 1,204 acre Manasquan Reservoir nearby.

What do Census figures show about housing in Howell?

Howell is firmly a township of owners: QuickFacts puts owner occupancy at 88.8 percent, the highest of the four places in its comparison table. The median owned home is valued at $507,200. Typical monthly costs are $2,846 for owners with a mortgage and $1,133 for those without.

Households number 19,134, each with 2.81 people on average, and median household income is $134,854. The poverty rate is 6.8 percent. Retail sales came to $23,830 per resident in 2022, far above the other three places in the same table, and shopping centers line Route 9. The 2020 count was 53,537 people, and the estimate for July 2025 is 55,156.

Residents 65 and older make up 17.2 percent of the township, and 89.3 percent of people stayed at one address through the prior year. A house needing work still sells, and a buyer who accepts its condition shortens the path.

How do Howell residents get to work and school?

Most working residents leave the township. The state labor department places Howell in the Monmouth-Ocean labor area, and more than 70 percent of employed residents work outside it, per the township's encyclopedia entry. Health care and social assistance employs 16.3 percent, retail 13.8 percent and education 11.1 percent.

  • Roads: Interstate 195, U.S. 9, Route 33 and Route 34 all cross the township, plus County Routes 524, 547 and 549. The Garden State Parkway is reached from I-195 and Route 33 at exits 98 and 100.
  • Buses: NJ Transit routes 131, 135 and 139 head to the Port Authority Bus Terminal. Resident-only park-and-ride lots sit at Aldrich, in Land of Pines, and in Adelphia. Belmar is the nearest train station.
  • Schools: the Howell Township district serves pre-kindergarten through grade 8 in 12 schools with 6,045 students in 2024-25. High schoolers attend Howell, Freehold Township or Colts Neck High School in the Freehold Regional district depending on address.

Horse farms and nurseries remain part of the landscape, which is why rural lots and acreage show up in local listings.

What does the Howell Fire Bureau require before a house changes hands?

Howell uses a Certificate of Smoke Alarm, Carbon Monoxide Alarm and Secondary Power Source Compliance for resales, handled by the Fire Bureau at 4567 Highway 9 North, second floor. Clean and test every alarm before the inspector arrives. The required type depends on when the house was built or renovated.

Smoke alarm minimums by construction date, from the Howell Fire Bureau compliance requirements sheet
Built or renovatedMinimum alarms
Before 197710 year sealed battery alarms on all levels
January 1977 to September 1978Electric alarm on each sleeping level, sealed battery elsewhere
October 1978 to January 1983Electric on sleeping level and basement, sealed battery elsewhere
February 1983 to July 1984Electric alarms on all levels
August 1984 to February 1991Electric on all levels, interconnected
March 1991 onwardElectric on every level and in each bedroom, interconnected, with battery backup

The sheet adds more details sellers miss.

  • Alarms must be under 10 years old by manufacture date, and replacing electric alarms with battery models is not allowed.
  • One and two family homes with a fuel-burning appliance or an attached garage need carbon monoxide alarms on each sleeping level and near every bedroom door.
  • A solar array, generator or battery system calls for a printed label reading CAUTION: MULTIPLE SOURCES OF POWER within 18 inches of the main panel and the meter.
  • House numbers must be at least 4 inches tall, contrast with the background and be visible from the street.
  • The sheet drops the old extinguisher rule for one and two family homes that change hands.

The Fire Bureau's number is 732-938-4500, extension 2900.

How do Howell property tax appeals and payoffs work?

Monmouth County follows a different calendar from most of New Jersey, so a Howell appeal is due January 15 rather than April 1. The state's appeals page lists Monmouth County alongside Burlington and Gloucester, and gives the Monmouth County Board of Taxation number as 732-431-7404. Appeals are filed on Form A-1 with that board.

If the board's judgment disappoints you, the Tax Court of New Jersey must receive your appeal within 45 days of that judgment. Owners of property assessed over $1,000,000 can skip the board and file with the Tax Court.

The township forms page lists Tax Collector requests for lien redemption figures, bank code removal and prepaid taxes. Ask for a redemption figure early if the house has a tax lien, since the payoff has to be in the closing statement.

Who records a Howell deed and what do the state rules add?

Deeds for a Howell sale are recorded by the Monmouth County Clerk, whose site lists real property recordings, e-recording and a recording fee schedule. Your title company normally files the deed and the tax forms together.

The seller pays the State Realty Transfer Fee. A sale at Howell's median value of $507,200 lands in the over-$350,000 schedule, where $4.80 per $500 applies between $200,000 and $550,000. Sellers who remain in the state sign GIT/REP-3. Someone relocating out of New Jersey becomes a nonresident for tax purposes on this sale, and an estimated payment of 2 percent of the price or 8.97 percent of the gain may come due at the table unless an exemption covers it.

More questions about Howell, NJ

What inspection does Howell require before I sell?

A smoke alarm, carbon monoxide alarm and secondary power source compliance inspection by the Howell Fire Bureau. The alarm type required depends on the year the house was built or renovated. Test and clean the alarms first, then confirm the appointment with the bureau at 732-938-4500, extension 2900.

Do I need fire extinguishers to sell a Howell home?

No, for a one or two family dwelling. According to the Fire Bureau's sheet, extinguishers no longer come into play when ownership or occupancy changes in those homes and in attached single-family units. Alarms, carbon monoxide detectors and any power-source label do still need to pass.

When is the deadline to appeal a Howell tax assessment?

January 15, because Monmouth County follows an alternative assessment calendar. Most other New Jersey counties use April 1. File Form A-1 with the Monmouth County Board of Taxation, and call that office at 732-431-7404 if you are unsure which date applies to your parcel.

Which county office records the deed on a Howell sale?

The Monmouth County Clerk. The office handles real property recordings and e-recording, and its website carries the recording fee schedule. Closing is where the deed, the transfer fee affidavit and the GIT/REP form usually get bundled and sent in by the title agent.

Can I sell a Howell house with tenants in it?

Yes. The township keeps rental forms, including a combined rental certificate, a landlord registration for multi-unit property and a single unit rental application. Pull those filings and the current lease before you list, since buyers on either side will want to see the terms.

What is it like to sell a house in Barnegat Township?

Barnegat Township in Ocean County is a fast-growing, mostly owner-occupied community where sellers deal with a township resale letter, a smoke and carbon monoxide certificate and, in many cases, environmental approvals tied to the location of the lot. It covers about 34 square miles of land between the Garden State Parkway corridor and Barnegat Bay.

Because nearly nine in ten homes are owner-occupied, most sales here are between households rather than investors. The sections below cover the local numbers, the township paperwork and the county steps that follow a signed contract.

How has Barnegat grown, and what do the housing numbers show?

The township reached 24,296 residents in the 2020 census, up from 20,936 in 2010, and the Census Bureau estimates 26,151 by mid-2025. That is a 7.6% rise over the estimate base for April 2020. Wikipedia notes that the 2020 count was the highest in the township's history.

With nearly nine in ten homes owner-occupied and almost a third of residents 65 or older, many sales here involve downsizing, estates or a move to be near family. Residents under 18 make up 17.6% of the population, and density has climbed to 709.6 people per square mile from 609.0 in 2010.

Where is Barnegat, and what shapes its history and layout?

Barnegat is a township in Ocean County, incorporated in 1846 as Union Township from parts of Dover and Stafford, and renamed Barnegat Township effective January 1, 1977. The name traces to Dutch explorers who mapped Barnegat Inlet in 1614, and the early spelling is usually translated as "inlet of the breakers."

The township includes the Barnegat census-designated place, part of Ocean Acres, which it shares with Stafford Township, and smaller localities such as Cedar Bridge, Howardsville, Lower Dock and Upper Dock. Barnegat borders Lacey, Little Egg Harbor, Long Beach, Ocean and Stafford townships in Ocean County, plus Bass River and Woodland townships in Burlington County. The Battle of Cedar Bridge, a skirmish near the Cedar Bridge Tavern in 1782, is one of the township's best-known historical events.

Which roads and schools matter to Barnegat buyers?

The Garden State Parkway runs north to south near the middle of the township, and U.S. Route 9 runs through the eastern side. New Jersey Route 72 and County Route 539 serve the western part, while County Route 554 crosses the township west to east. NJ Transit bus route 559 connects the area with Atlantic City, and the census puts the average commute at 27.8 minutes.

Public school students attend the Barnegat Township School District, which Wikipedia lists with six schools and 3,583 students in 2021-22. Include the district name and your bus or school-zone details in your listing, since buyers with children ask first.

  • Route 9 and Route 72 frontage can trigger state highway approvals for work on the lot.
  • About 31% of residents are 65 or older, which keeps single-level homes and low-maintenance lots in demand.

What paperwork does Barnegat Township require for a home sale?

Barnegat Township requires a Letter of No Interest on resales, according to the Code Enforcement page, and the Forms page lists a Resale Complete Letter of No Interest and a state smoke detector and carbon monoxide certification. Call the township's Rentals and Resales line at 609-698-0080, extension 159, before you list.

The township's construction office also handles permit history, which matters if you finished a basement, built a deck or added a shed. Unpermitted work can slow a sale, so ask the office whether your permits were closed. The township routes calls by extension on the same main line: construction permits at 135, 150 and 153, the planning and zoning board at 155, and the fire, electrical and plumbing subcodes at 157, 158 and 115. Having the right extension saves a round of transfers when a buyer's inspector asks for sign-offs.

  • Zoning permits cover sheds, fences, decks, pools, driveways, patios and additions.
  • A fence needs a zoning permit and a survey or plot plan from a licensed New Jersey surveyor.
  • Tree clearing permits are required before cutting trees.
  • Vacant properties must be registered with the township, and the forms page carries both registration and de-registration forms.

Do Pinelands, DEP or septic rules affect a sale in Barnegat?

They can, depending on where the lot sits. The township's construction office lists the prior approvals that come before local permits: Pinelands approval for land west of the Parkway only, state environmental approval for waterfront and freshwater wetland areas, and Department of Transportation approval for Route 9 and Route 72 properties.

The same page lists county health department approval for septic systems, wells and food handling, and county soil conservation district review for soil disturbance of 5,000 square feet or more. If your house is on septic, ask a buyer's inspector which records they will want. If part of your lot lies west of the Parkway, tell your agent early so buyers understand what Pinelands rules may mean for later projects.

What if I rent the house or my buyer is a senior?

Rental properties in Barnegat need a certificate of occupancy before every new tenant and must be registered with the municipal clerk. Units rented for fewer than 30 days need a yearly certificate, and failure to file can bring a summons to the owner.

On the state side, New Jersey publishes a reduced realty transfer fee schedule for senior citizens, blind or disabled persons, and for low and moderate income housing. The standard sale above $350,000 starts at $2.90 per $500 for the first $150,000, while the reduced schedule starts at $1.40. Ask your closing agent whether the transaction qualifies. The township's forms page also lists affordable housing applications for purchase and rental, which matters if your house sits in a program.

Where is the deed recorded and who pays the transfer fees?

Deeds for Barnegat sales are recorded with the Ocean County Clerk, whose office handles land records and property search for the county. The seller pays the state realty transfer fee when the deed goes on record, and a seller who lives out of state also files a GIT/REP form and prepays at least 2% of the deed consideration.

Plan for these items on closing day: the payoff of any mortgage, the transfer fee, township certificate costs and any unpaid taxes or water and sewer charges. A cash buyer or a title company can walk through those lines before you sign.

More questions about Barnegat, NJ

Does Barnegat Township require anything special to sell a house?

Yes. The township asks for a Letter of No Interest on resales, and sellers also need the state smoke and carbon monoxide certification. Call the Rentals and Resales line at 609-698-0080, extension 159, to confirm current steps.

Is Barnegat mostly owner-occupied?

Yes. The Census Bureau reports an 88.0% owner-occupied rate for 2020-2024, with a median home value of $399,000, so most sales are between homeowners.

Do Pinelands rules apply to every Barnegat property?

No. The township lists Pinelands approval for land west of the Garden State Parkway only. Lots east of the Parkway may still need state environmental approval if they are on the water or near wetlands.

Which roads serve Barnegat Township?

The Garden State Parkway crosses the middle of the township, and U.S. Route 9 runs through the east. Route 72 and County Route 539 serve the west, and County Route 554 crosses west to east.

Who pays the realty transfer fee on a Barnegat sale?

The seller does. The state sets the fee by sale price in steps per $500, the county clerk collects it with the deed, and seniors may qualify for a reduced schedule.

What are the realistic ways to close a sale in Berkeley Township?

Owners here generally pick among a broker listing, a do-it-yourself sale and an as-is cash purchase. Whatever you pick, the township wants a Certificate of Occupancy for the resale, and a house inside an age-restricted community also needs an approval letter from its homeowners association.

Berkeley's population skews old: people 65 and over are 42.6 percent of the total. That makes many sales a downsizing move, a transfer to assisted living or heirs clearing out a parent's place. A listing rewards a tidy house and a seller who can sit through showings and a buyer's loan approval. A cash buyer is the more practical match for an estate, a place that needs work or an owner who has already relocated.

  • Broker listing: most buyers see it, you pay a commission and negotiate repairs.
  • Do-it-yourself sale: you arrange the inspection, the certificate and the attorney.
  • Cash purchase: condition is the buyer's problem, and the price reflects the repair bill.

What is the land like in Berkeley Township?

Berkeley covers 54.25 square miles, and 11.53 of those are water, about 21 percent of the total. The township stretches from the Atlantic shore and Barnegat Bay west into the Pine Barrens. About 72 percent of its land lies inside the Pinelands National Reserve, and the barrier island section holds Island Beach State Park and South Seaside Park.

The township was incorporated on March 31, 1875, out of Dover Township, which is now Toms River Township. It surrounds the borough of Ocean Gate and touches Toms River, Lacey, Manchester, Beachwood, Pine Beach, Island Heights and the Seaside communities. The Pinewald area began as a 1920s resort plan that sold about 8,000 lots in 1928 and 1929, and the Holiday City, Holiday Heights and Silver Ridge developments added the age-restricted housing that shapes much of the township.

That geography matters for a sale. Bay and river frontage, flood maps and Pinelands rules can shape what a buyer's lender, insurer or surveyor asks for. If your lot touches the water or the preserved woodland, gather survey and flood paperwork before you list.

Who lives in Berkeley Township, and what do homes cost?

Berkeley counted 45,550 residents as of July 2025, a 4.1 percent gain on the 2020 base. The typical household has only 2.01 people, a pattern that fits a retirement community. Nearly nine in ten homes (88.9 percent) are owner-occupied, and homes in that group have a median value of $310,000 in the latest five-year survey.

On money: a household brings in $66,008 at the median, per person the figure is $48,539, and renters pay $1,683 at the median. Owners with a mortgage spend $1,925 a month at the median, and those without one spend $661. The average commute takes 33.9 minutes.

Which township approvals does a Berkeley Township resale need?

According to the Township's Rental and Resale Inspections page, a Certificate of Occupancy is needed every time a Berkeley home is sold or rented. For a transfer, rental or resale in an age-restricted community, the page adds that an original approval letter from the homeowners association must accompany the application, bearing a live signature and not a duplicate.

Inspectors apply the township's written rules for battery-powered smoke and carbon monoxide alarms. Separately, state rules call for a compliance certificate before a one- or two-unit house is sold, available only from the municipality. Town Hall sits at 627 Pinewald-Keswick Road in Bayville; call 732-244-7400 for the current forms.

  • File the resale application the week a contract is signed.
  • Find out from the association how long its letter takes to issue.
  • Confirm that decks, additions and finished basements each have a final inspection on file.
  • Test every alarm against the township's written requirements before the inspector arrives.

How does Berkeley Township collect property tax?

Bills go out once a year, normally in July. Two quarters are billed as estimates, and the other two are adjusted so the year adds up to the real tax. The Ocean County Board of Taxation sets the rate once the township, the school districts and the county file certified budgets.

Berkeley Township installment and penalty rules, as published by its Tax Collector
RuleWhat the Tax Collector's page says
InstallmentsQuarterly, beginning each February 1 and continuing through November 1
GraceA 10-day window after every installment date
Interest8 percent applies to the first $1,500 of a late payment, and 18 percent to the remainder
Added penalty6 percent once a delinquency passes $10,000
Still unpaidGoes into the tax sale after year-end under state statute
How to payOnline, by ACH debit, at the Town Hall counter or in the lock box outside the building

In a mid-year sale the closing statement divides that quarter's tax by days of ownership. Before closing, have the Tax Collector's office confirm what is owed so no installment remains open under your name.

What is happening with South Seaside Park?

Residents of this barrier island neighborhood petitioned in 2014 to leave Berkeley Township for the borough of Seaside Park, pointing out that they live 16 miles from the township's municipal offices. The New Jersey Supreme Court sided with them in 2025.

Following guidance from the Attorney General's Office, the Tax Collector says taxes on South Seaside Park properties remain payable to Berkeley Township through the end of 2026, and that any change in collection starts January 1, 2027. An owner there should confirm with both municipalities which office issues the resale approval and the tax bill for the year of the closing.

How do roads and schools affect a Berkeley Township sale?

Garden State Parkway exits 77 and 80 serve the township. Route 9 crosses the east-central area, Route 35 clips it and ends at the Island Beach State Park road, and a short stretch of Route 37 touches the township. Of about 266 miles of roadway, the township maintains 220.88. NJ Transit bus 559 links to Atlantic City, and Ocean Ride operates routes OC1, OC2, OC7 and OC8.

Four schools in the Berkeley Township School District teach pre-kindergarten through sixth grade to 2,385 students (2024 to 2025). Seventh through twelfth graders go to Central Regional Middle School and Central Regional High School. Just 11.6 percent of residents are under 18, so age-restriction rules and single-level layouts tend to drive buyer questions more than school ratings.

Is a cash buyer worth considering in Berkeley Township?

A cash buyer is worth a call when certainty matters more than the top price: deferred maintenance, an association whose approval drags, or an estate with several heirs. The buyer may still have to secure the township certificate and the association letter, so decide in writing who files and who pays.

Judge any offer against a realistic listing net. Subtract commission, repair credits and the months of tax, association dues and utilities you would carry while waiting. A New Jersey attorney should read the contract and the deed language before you sign.

More questions about Berkeley, NJ

Is a resale inspection mandatory in Berkeley Township?

Yes. Every sale needs a township Certificate of Occupancy, and landlords need one each time a tenant changes. Have working alarms for smoke and carbon monoxide in place before the inspector visits.

What does an age-restricted community add to a Berkeley sale?

An original letter of approval from the homeowners association. The township does not take copies, and the letter must carry an original signature, so request it once a buyer is lined up.

What are the Berkeley Township tax installment dates?

Quarterly: February 1, then May 1, August 1 and finally November 1, each followed by 10 grace days. Late interest is 8 percent on the first $1,500 and 18 percent beyond it, with a 6 percent penalty once a delinquency tops $10,000.

Where do South Seaside Park owners send their property tax?

To Berkeley Township through the end of 2026. The township states that any change in collection takes effect January 1, 2027, so confirm the arrangement with the Tax Collector before a closing.

Can a senior seller pay less in New Jersey realty transfer fee?

Possibly. Senior citizens, blind persons and disabled persons can claim a partial exemption, which is personal and not available to a trust or an estate. The Division of Taxation's example shows a $475 fee on a $280,000 sale by a qualifying senior, and your attorney files the seller affidavit.

What are the quickest ways to sell in Brick Township?

A seller in Brick has three realistic paths: hire an agent, handle the sale alone, or sign with a cash buyer who purchases the property untouched. Cash moves fastest and generally pays least. Listing adds commission and fix-up costs and takes longer. The right choice turns on the roof, the flood history, your deadline, and what the house would net after each route.

Ocean County's Brick Township was estimated at 77,402 people in mid-2025, up 5.1% from the 2020 base, per the Census Bureau. That growth, in a place that lost population between 2000 and 2020, means buyers are active, but the housing stock is mostly decades old. Many sellers meet the same questions: flood zones, inspection paperwork, and quarterly tax bills.

What kind of housing market is Brick Township?

Brick is a mature shore suburb where owners dominate. The 2020-2024 survey counts 30,289 households, 82.2% of them owning, with a $410,600 median home value and $106,130 median income. Rent runs $1,756 a month at the median, so a rental is a realistic fallback for some owners but not a cheap one to maintain under the township's inspection rules.

The township covers 25.59 square miles of land plus a lot of water. The mainland sits along the Metedeconk River and Barnegat Bay, and a separate set of ocean beaches (Brick Ocean Beaches I, II and III) lies on the barrier peninsula. Because the two parts do not touch, a street address can mean very different insurance and elevation questions. Older neighborhoods such as Laurelton, Lake Riviera and Baywood grew after the Garden State Parkway opened in 1954 and a building boom ran through the 1980s.

  • Many homes date from the 1950s through the 1980s, so roofs, septic or sewer connections, and electrical panels are common negotiation points.
  • Waterfront and bayfront lots near Cherry Quay, Havens Cove and Shore Acres carry their own flood and elevation questions.
  • Herbertsville and Parkway Pines sit near Parkway exit 91, away from the rest of the township, and attract commuters.

How does flood risk change a Brick home sale?

Flood history is the single biggest local variable. Hurricane Sandy in October 2012 devastated parts of Brick, and barrier island and waterfront properties took the worst of it; some buildings had to be torn down. A February 2026 blizzard also dropped roughly two feet of snow and knocked out power in several areas, which is a reminder that roofs and heating systems matter even away from the water.

The township's floodplain information page says it provides flood zone data to realtors, lenders, insurers and owners, including base flood elevation, whether a lot is in a coastal barrier area, and whether flood insurance is mandatory. Elevation certificates on file can be searched through the township's mapping tool, or requested from the engineering office by address or block and lot. Pull the certificate before you list, because a buyer's lender will ask for it.

Brick takes part in the federal Community Rating System, which can lower flood premiums. Its floodplain plan lists 140 mitigation initiatives, 81 of them completed by the latest annual report. A seller who can show an elevation certificate, a recent flood policy, and any raised-utility work usually faces fewer price cuts.

Which schools and roads do Brick buyers ask about?

Brick Public Schools serves pre-kindergarten through grade 12 inside the township. The district ran 12 schools and about 8,414 students in 2020-21, with elementary schools such as Drum Point, Lanes Mill, Midstreams, Osbornville, Veterans Memorial and Emma Havens Young, two middle schools (Lake Riviera and Veterans Memorial), and two high schools: Brick Memorial and Brick Township High School. Buyers often check which elementary zone a street falls in, so mention it in the listing.

The Garden State Parkway crosses the western side with exits 89, 90 and 91. Routes 70, 88 and 35 and county routes 528 and 549 handle local traffic. The old Laurelton Circle at Routes 70 and 88 once carried about 95,000 vehicles a day before it became a signal-controlled intersection in 1986. NJ Transit runs the 137 bus to the Port Authority Bus Terminal in Manhattan and the 67 to Newark, and a Park and Ride at exit 91 serves express commuters. Average commute time for workers is 28.2 minutes.

What township paperwork applies when a Brick house is sold or rented?

Brick's Division of Inspections, which is the Building Department, issues construction permits and handles requests for certificates under the New Jersey Uniform Construction Code. Open or unclosed permits are the usual cause of delay at closing, so have the division confirm the status of past work before you sign. The building office answers permit and certificate questions by voicemail and email, listed in the table below.

Brick also treats rental homes strictly. Owners must register the landlord with the clerk, apply for a Rental Certificate of Occupancy, and file a mercantile license with proof of at least $500,000 in liability coverage. Code Enforcement then inspects every rental each year, at $100 per inspection and $50 per failed re-inspection. The annual checklist covers smoke and carbon monoxide detectors, ground-fault outlets near water, a mounted fire extinguisher, and lead-safe status for structures built before 1978. Since September 27, 2022, creditors must also register foreclosed or vacant residential and commercial properties with the township within 10 days of filing a foreclosure action.

How are Brick property taxes billed, and what happens at closing?

Brick's tax year follows the calendar, with installments falling on the first of February, May, August and November and a ten-day grace window after each. Each bill covers a calendar quarter (the February bill pays for January through March), which matters at closing because the seller owes tax only through the closing date. A missing bill is no defense against interest, the tax collector warns, so make sure the closing agent has the current quarter's figure.

Work done on the house can add a second layer. After construction is finished, the township places an assessment on the improvement and mails an Added Assessment Bill in October, due November 1 and again on February 1 and May 1 of the following year. A seller who finished a deck or addition should ask the assessor whether that bill is still coming.

  • Assessment notices go out each year, usually by February 1, and an owner who thinks the value is wrong may appeal on or before April 1 to the Ocean County Board of Taxation.
  • Properties assessed above $1,000,000 can file directly with the State Tax Court of New Jersey.
  • The assessor processes veteran and senior or disabled deductions, each currently $250.

What does New Jersey charge a seller on a house sale?

The state's Realty Transfer Fee is the seller's cost, collected as the deed goes on record. On a standard sale of $350,000 or less, the rate is $2.00 per $500 on the first $150,000, $3.35 on the next $50,000, and $3.90 on the remainder. Above $350,000 the schedule starts at $2.90 and climbs to $4.80 per $500 between $200,000 and $550,000. At Brick's median value of roughly $410,600, most sales land in that second schedule. For the exact figure on your price, use the Division of Taxation rate tables.

Closing costs also include deed recording, any payoff of liens, and whatever the buyer negotiates for repairs. A cash buyer typically absorbs repairs, so the realistic comparison is your net after repairs, carrying costs through the winter, and agent fees against a single offer with a closing date you choose.

Is a cash sale the right call for a Brick homeowner?

A cash sale fits best when the home has defects an inspector would flag, when flood or storm damage is unrepaired, when the owner has inherited a house in another town, or when quarterly tax bills and a mortgage are piling up. It also helps landlords who do not want to carry the annual rental inspection cycle. It makes less sense for a move-in-ready home on a good street where a listing will draw several offers.

Whatever the buyer, get the offer on paper, set it beside the proceeds of a listing after commission, and confirm who pays for the certificate and recording steps. If you are close to a foreclosure filing, speak to a housing counselor or attorney in addition to any buyer, because the township's vacant property registration and the lender's timeline both affect your options.

More questions about Brick, NJ

Can I sell my Brick house if it was damaged in a storm?

Yes. Houses with storm damage change hands regularly, mostly to investors and cash buyers who subtract the repair bill. Collect your elevation certificate, flood claim paperwork and permit history first. The engineering office can look up certificates by address or by block and lot.

Which Brick office handles permits and certificates?

Start with the Division of Inspections voicemail line, 732-262-4604, or the permit status email on the township's building page. Rental certificate matters belong to Code Enforcement, 732-262-1033, weekdays.

What is the cutoff for contesting a Brick assessment?

April 1 each year, filed with the Ocean County Board of Taxation. Owners of property assessed above $1,000,000 may file directly with the State Tax Court of New Jersey instead.

Does a landlord need a certificate before selling a rented house in Brick?

A landlord needs the Rental Certificate of Occupancy to keep tenants in place, and the township inspects each rental every year. Ask the Division of Inspections what is required for your property when the sale closes and whether tenants move out first.

Who pays the realty transfer fee on a Brick sale?

The seller pays it. Recording the deed triggers the charge, which follows the price written in the deed and the Division of Taxation's published rates. Sales above $1,000,000 add a graduated percent fee.

Last updated November 14, 2026.

Bernards at a glance

Selling in Bernards?

Get My Cash Offer →

What are the routes to a closing for a Bernards Township house?

A Bernards Township owner can put the house on the market, sell it to a buyer found privately, or accept a cash bid for the property as it stands. The township layers its own pre-sale steps over state rules, so the actual pace depends on how quickly permits and inspections get cleared.

With homes valued around $814,800 at the median, many buyers finance, and a listing draws them. A cash bid answers different problems: an inherited house in Basking Ridge, a property whose permits were never closed, a rental after the tenant leaves, or a seller who needs a date that will hold.

  • Agent listing: the highest potential price, a longer timeline and repair talks after the inspection.
  • Private sale: no agent fee, with pricing, marketing and township paperwork on your desk.
  • Cash buyer: condition does not stall the sale, and the bid is reduced for the work required.

How do the Census numbers describe Bernards Township homeowners?

Housing values here sit far above the national median of $332,700. The Census Bureau puts the township at 28,594 residents in July 2025. Owners live in 83.1 percent of the housing units. Households bring in $194,107 at the median and $109,797 per person, and rent at the median is $2,476.

Adults here are highly educated, with 74.2 percent holding a bachelor's degree or higher. Foreign-born residents are 25.3 percent of the population, and 24.1 percent of people are under 18. A language other than English is spoken at home by 29.4 percent of those age 5 and up. Monthly owner costs reach the top bracket the survey reports: $4,000 or more with a mortgage, $1,500 or more without one.

At these price levels buyers expect a clean permit file, and the township checks for one before any residential sale anyway.

Where is Bernards Township and what is it made of?

Bernards sits at the eastern end of the Somerset Hills and covers 24.33 square miles, nearly all of it land. The Second Watchung Mountain bounds the southwest, the Dead River swamp lies to the south, and the Great Swamp National Wildlife Refuge, the Passaic River and Millington Gorge form the eastern edge. Within the township are Basking Ridge, Liberty Corner, Lyons, Franklin Corners, Mount Horeb, Madisonville and part of The Hills, and the Martinsville ZIP Code 08836 covers a piece of it too.

The area was chartered in 1760 as Bernardston Township and incorporated as Bernards Township on February 21, 1798. Far Hills split off in 1921 and Bernardsville in 1924. Voters turned down a borough of Basking Ridge by better than four to one. The township now has 138.86 miles of roads and neighbors Bedminster, Bernardsville, Bridgewater, Warren, Harding and Long Hill.

What must a Bernards Township seller obtain before closing?

Two things, both issued from 277 South Maple Avenue in Basking Ridge. The first is an inspection and certification of smoke detectors, carbon monoxide detectors and a fire extinguisher from the Bureau of Fire Prevention. The second is a Construction Records Clearance from the Code Enforcement Division. The township's selling guide, revised June 2026, says to create a free account on its online portal to apply.

The clearance rule in the township code says a Construction Records Clearance is required before the sale of any residential structure, and both owner and purchaser can be held responsible if one is not issued. The inspector checks records for open construction or zoning permits, and any open permit must have its final inspection before the clearance issues. File at least 10 business days before the change of ownership. A violation carries a fine up to $1,000, up to 90 days in jail or up to 90 days of community service.

Construction Records Clearance fees in Bernards Township
When the request reaches the townshipFee
More than 10 calendar days before closing or change of occupancy$40
Within 10 calendar days of closing or change of occupancy$75
Within 4 calendar days of closing or change of occupancy$125
  • Create the free account on the township's online portal and file both applications.
  • Close any open construction or zoning permit before the records inspection.
  • Schedule the fire safety inspection for smoke detectors, carbon monoxide detectors and the extinguisher.
  • Send the clearance fee with the application, using the tier that matches your closing date.

The code exempts several transfers when no one changes occupancy, including title corrections, a transfer between spouses and a transfer by or to an executor or administrator distributing an estate. Mortgage refinancing and home equity loans are exempt as well.

How are Bernards Township property taxes set and paid?

The Tax Collector posts a 2026 total rate of $1.661. Of that, $0.275 funds the county, $0.030 county open space, $1.077 the school district, $0.246 the municipality and $0.033 the library. Four installments fall on the first of February, May, August and November, and the 10th of each of those months is the last day of grace. Postmarks do not count; the payment must be physically in the office.

Collections reached 99.50 percent of the 2025 levy across 10,358 tax accounts and 7,231 sewer accounts counted on January 1, 2026. Sewer bills follow their own cycle, due January 1 and July 1 with a 30-day grace period. A closing in the middle of a quarter is prorated, so get a current balance on both the tax and sewer accounts.

Veteran and senior deductions exist. Seniors qualify at 65 or older on October 1 of the prior year, if they live in the home and stay under the income limit; tell your attorney if a deduction is in place.

Do floods affect a sale in Bernards Township?

They can. The Passaic River runs along the township's edge, and the township keeps a flood information page with flood zone maps for buildings, floodways, open space and township property. It also lists its National Flood Insurance Program Class 7 approval and links to FEMA maps and elevation guides.

Ask a buyer's lender whether the property needs flood insurance, and look up the parcel on the township and FEMA maps before you list. A seller who can show an elevation certificate or a clear zone designation answers a common buyer question in the first week.

What do transit, roads and schools add to Bernards Township listings?

Interstate 78, Interstate 287 and U.S. Route 202 serve the township. NJ Transit's Gladstone Branch stops at Basking Ridge and Lyons stations on the way to Hoboken Terminal, and Lakeland Bus Lines runs a Route 78 rush-hour service from Bedminster to the Port Authority Bus Terminal. Mean travel time to work is 32.5 minutes.

The Bernards Township School District runs six schools, among them Cedar Hill, Liberty Corner, Mount Prospect and Oak Street elementary schools, William Annin Middle School and Ridge High School. Ridge High School won a National Blue Ribbon award in 2009 to 2010. The district reported 4,874 students in 2020 to 2021. Private options include Pingry School's upper campus in Basking Ridge and Saint James School.

What changes when a Bernards Township buyer pays cash?

Paying cash takes out the lender's appraisal and most repair haggling. The Construction Records Clearance, the Bureau of Fire Prevention certification and the state transfer fee all stay in place. Agree up front who files each application, because the clearance fee climbs as closing nears.

Weigh offers by what you keep. A listing may fetch more, but commission, staging, inspection credits and holding costs come out of it. Above $1,000,000 the buyer owes an extra 1 percent fee beyond the seller's own transfer fee.

More questions about Bernards, NJ

Is a smoke detector certificate the only thing Bernards Township asks for?

No. The Code Enforcement Division also issues a Construction Records Clearance before a residential sale. Its review looks for open construction or zoning permits, which need final inspections before the clearance is released.

How much does a Construction Records Clearance cost in Bernards Township?

$40 if it reaches the township more than 10 calendar days ahead of closing, $75 inside 10 days and $125 inside 4 days. The township asks for the application at least 10 business days before ownership changes.

When are Bernards Township property taxes due?

The first of February, May, August and November, with grace through the 10th. The money must be in the Tax Collector's hands by then, since a postmark proves nothing. Sewer bills are due January 1 and July 1.

Which transfers skip the Bernards clearance?

A transfer is exempt when occupancy stays the same. The code lists a deed correction, a transfer between spouses, an estate distribution by an executor or administrator, and refinancing or home equity loans.

Does the buyer ever pay a transfer fee in New Jersey?

Only when the price is above $1,000,000. The seller pays the standard realty transfer fee in every sale, and the buyer owes an added 1 percent when consideration exceeds that line.
